Trump’s Fed nightmare: Rates won’t be slashed. They could surge now
If Donald Trump expects Kevin Warsh, his hand-picked chair of the US Federal Reserve Board, to deliver the interest rate cuts that he has continuously clamoured for, he is about to be disappointed, again.
It now appears inevitable that the Fed will deliver its second rate rise in this cycle – the first was in September – after the US inflation rate came in above expectations for the third successive month.
The only question – and just raising it will upset Trump – is whether the US central bank hikes its policy rate by 25 basis points or 50 basis points when it meets again next month.
The US Bureau of Labor Statistics said on Tuesday that consumer prices rose 0.4 per cent in October. While calculations are muddied by the fact that a government shutdown meant there was no data collected in October last year, most calculations put the annual inflation rate at 4 per cent.
Even if energy and food costs are excluded – which would remove the direct effects of the war in the Middle East on oil and fuel costs – “core” inflation in October was 0.3 per cent and the annual core inflation rate 2.8 per cent – well above the Fed’s target of 2 per cent.
Moreover, inflation is spreading across the US economy, thanks to Trump’s tariffs and the indirect effects of the higher oil and refined product prices on transport costs that are now feeding into goods and services prices.
The only question – and just raising it will upset Trump – is whether the US central bank hikes its policy rate by 25 basis points or 50 basis points when it meets again next month.
Fed officials are already preparing the ground for more than one rate hike.
Fed governor Christopher Waller (a Trump appointee) told an audience in London on Tuesday that, should the inflation rate for the month come in above 0.3 per cent, a half-percentage point (50 basis point) rate rise might be needed. A conventional 25 basis point rise, he argued, would do little to win confidence that the Fed was serious about tackling inflation.
Also on Tuesday, Dallas Fed president Lorie Logan said it was clear that the Fed needed to make “at least” two more 25 basis point rises and may need to move quicker than the bank had moved thus far.
Kansas City’s Fed president Jeffrey Schmid said he believed the central bank’s current stance was “fairly accommodative” while another Fed governor, Michelle Bowman, indicated that she, too, would support another rate rise.
Markets immediately priced in a 100 per cent probability of a 25 basis point rise in December as bond yields rose and the sharemarket fell.
The yield on two-year Treasury securities jumped 19 basis points – its biggest one-day rise since Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs were announced in April last year. The 10-year bond yield was also up, by 15 basis points to 5.01 per cent.
The inflation rate rose even though oil prices were mostly flat throughout the month. It would appear to be the delayed impacts of higher gasoline and, in particular diesel prices, that are now flowing through the economy and bleeding into consumer prices.
The oil price has fallen back this month to trade at around $US92 a barrel and gasoline prices are sliding, albeit that they are, at $US3.98 a gallon, still about 30 per cent higher than they were a year ago. Diesel prices are still 65 per cent higher than a year ago.
The oil price has been falling because oil flows from the Middle East have been restored to close to pre-war levels (albeit with far higher transport and insurance costs) and because Trump keeps saying that a negotiated end to the war is within reach, although he has said similar things throughout this year, but the conflict has yet to be resolved.
With the US midterm elections out of the way, the administration may, however, find it easier to accede to some of Iran’s demands.
Even if the oil price continues to retreat, however, refined product prices - of which diesel is the key product - are unlikely to subside as quickly, as the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine have significantly damaged refinery capacity.
The result of the midterms will help the Fed if it starts more aggressively raising US interest rates. That might infuriate the president, but there is little he can do about it.
If the wars were to end soon, it would still take well into next year for volumes to recover. In the meantime, the higher cost of transporting goods and food will continue to push up goods and grocery prices.
Tariffs remain another contributor to the inflation rate with their stop-start history, thanks to the courts consistently ruling them illegal and the Trump administration’s continuing efforts to reimpose them using new legislative headings. Toy prices, for instance, were 9 per cent higher than a year ago. Auto parts and repairs prices were up 0.6 per cent in October.
Then there’s the impact of the boom in artificial intelligence, which is pushing up the prices of semiconductors and impacting the prices of computers, smartphones and other devices as well as electricity prices.
The inflation data underscores why US voters gave the Republicans such a thrashing at the midterm elections. For ordinary US households, the cost-of-living pressures are real and intensifying.
The result of the midterms – a Democrat majority in both chambers of Congress – will help the Fed if it, as expected, starts more aggressively raising US interest rates. That might infuriate a president who wanted Warsh to deliver greatly lower rates, but there is little he can do about it.
Trump has tried, unsuccessfully, to remove former Fed chair Jerome Powell from the board, threatening to prosecute him for cost overruns in the renovations of the Fed’s Washington headquarters. He’s still trying to unseat another governor, Lisa Cook, with flimsy accusations of mortgage fraud.
Even if he were able to sack Cook (there is a handpicked administration panel “investigating” her), or Powell decided to retire before his term ends in January 2028, the Democrats are most unlikely to approve a new Trump nomination to the board. And other Fed governors are now less likely to feel intimidated by potential administration responses to votes in favour of rate rises.
It’s not been a good week for Trump and his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. On Monday, the Congressional Budget Office released its summary of the outcomes from the 2026 fiscal year which, in the US, ends on September 30.
The Trump administration presided over a deficit of $US2 trillion ($2.9 trillion), or 6.2 per cent of GDP, a significant increase from the $US1.8 trillion (5.8 per cent of GDP) deficit in fiscal 2025.
The administration is spending more (outlays were up 6 per cent) while, thanks to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s tax cuts for companies and the wealthy, generating only 3 per cent revenue growth. Corporate tax revenue fell 16 per cent. Customs revenue fell 11 per cent because the administration had to refund $US126 billion after the US Supreme Court deemed Trump’s original global tariffs illegal.
America’s finances aren’t improving. In October, the CBO estimates, there was a deficit of $US409 billion, 30 per cent more than the same month last year, with revenues shrinking and spending growing.
With government debt of more than $US40 trillion and the net interest cost of that debt rising 11 per cent in the year to September, to $US1.14 trillion, a rising rate environment would only increase the threat to America’s financial stability and its ability to sustain even its modest, by comparison with other developed economies, social security net.
Bessent, who promised to lower the deficit-to-GDP ratio to 3 per cent, now says economic growth will fix America’s public finances.
It won’t, and Trump’s second term will, like his first term, leave a legacy of unfulfilled promises and unsustainable debt and deficits, with ordinary Americans much poorer for the experience.

US Inflation Rises Another 0.4% Ahead of Holidays
US inflation tops forecasts, fueling December Fed rate hike bets
sources.text:
U.S. consumer prices rose faster than expected in October as higher food and housing costs fueled inflationary pressures, strengthening expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its December policy meeting.
The Consumer Price Index report from the Labor Department on Tuesday also showed a strong buildup of underlying inflation pressures for a third straight month. It followed data last week showing the labor market regained momentum in October.
Inflation is being driven by the US-Israeli war with Iran, which has boosted oil prices, the Trump administration's import tariffs, resilient consumer spending and aggressive business investment in artificial intelligence technology.
The rising cost of living contributed to the heavy losses suffered by President Donald Trump's Republican Party in the midterm elections last week.
Fed Governor Christopher Waller said on Tuesday the US central bank should raise rates next month, adding that "a stronger policy move may be needed." Waller also raised the prospect of an aggressive 50-basis-point hike.
"The Fed seems to be falling behind the curve on inflation, and the October hold is looking like a policy mistake," said Stephen Juneau, an economist at Bank of America Securities. "We see a rising risk that the Fed will have to hike again in January, rather than March."
The CPI increased 0.4% last month after advancing 0.6% in September, the department's Bureau of Labor Statistics said. It was the third consecutive month of gains of 0.4% or more. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the CPI would climb 0.3% over the month. The BLS did not publish year-over-year inflation readings because last year's federal government shutdown prevented the collection of consumer price data in October 2025, leaving no comparison base.
Some economists used the average index for September and November 2025 to estimate the year-over-year rate of change for the October CPI. Others used interpolated levels from independent sources. Their estimates for the October year-over-year CPI ranged from a gain of 3.9% to 4.0%. Annual consumer inflation was 3.7% in September.
Shelter, which includes rents and hotel and motel rooms, accounted for more than 30% of the monthly increase in the CPI. Shelter costs rose 0.3% after climbing 0.4% in September.
Food prices surged 0.5% after barely rising in the prior three months. Grocery store prices climbed 0.4%, boosted by a 0.9% jump in the cost of beef. Egg prices rose 0.6%, while fruits and vegetables were 0.6% more expensive. Prices for dairy products increased 0.6%. The cost of snacks surged 1.0%.
Rising prices at the supermarket could be an early sign that high diesel prices are filtering through to consumers. The cost of eating out also increased last month, with prices of food away from home rising 0.5% after a 0.2% gain in September. The cost of full-service meals jumped 0.7%.
"This may finally be the beginning of a pass-through of higher transportation costs to grocery prices," said Stephen Stanley, chief US economist at Santander US Capital Markets. "If this is indeed happening, it could be a feature across a broad array of goods categories."
Gasoline prices climbed 1.0% after soaring 9.1% in September. Consumers also paid more for electricity. Although diesel prices have eased off all-time highs, they remain on an upward trend, rising 2.7% in October after increasing 11.9% in September.
Consumers could get some relief at the pump, with oil prices down at least 10% so far this month, but the pressure is unlikely to ease elsewhere, economists warned.
Inflation-adjusted average weekly earnings fell again in October.
The so-called core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy items, increased 0.3% in October for the third straight month. The so-called core CPI was forecast to have climbed 0.2% in October. Economists estimated that year-over-year core CPI inflation gained 2.8% in October. Annual core CPI inflation rose 2.6% in September.
Financial markets are pricing in a roughly 89% chance of a 25-basis-point rate hike next month, and expect another increase in March, CME Group's FedWatch tool showed. The Fed left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range last month. Economists said only a substantial selloff in equity markets or widening credit spreads would prevent the Fed from tightening monetary policy in December.
Stocks on Wall Street were trading lower. They slumped last week after the Democrats' sweeping victory fanned fears that new regulations could dent the durability of the AI trade, but rallied on Monday as oil prices fell. The dollar gained against a basket of currencies. US Treasury yields were mostly higher.
Underlying inflation last month was driven by a 0.3% rise in owners' equivalent rent, a measure of the amount homeowners would pay to rent or earn from renting their property. Prices for hotel and motel rooms rose 0.6%. Airline fares increased 0.4%. The cost of recreation services climbed 0.9%, while that of motor vehicle insurance advanced 0.7%.
Doctor visits and hospital services also cost more. But the price of health insurance dropped 1.8%. The BLS updated the data used to calculate this component. Overall services prices excluding energy increased 0.3% after rising 0.4% in September.
Tariff effects were also evident in October. Prices of household furnishings and supplies rebounded 0.7% and the cost of toys increased 1.8%. There were more price gains for computers and peripherals, reflecting the AI spending boom. Prices for smartphones rose a record 1.4%.
There were also increases in the prices of new vehicles and medication. But used car and truck prices dropped 1.2%. Core goods prices increased 0.2% after climbing 0.3% in September.
The missing data from last year have no impact on the calculation of the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index readings that the Fed tracks to gauge progress toward its inflation target.
Based on last month's data, economists estimated that core PCE inflation rose 0.4% after advancing 0.3% in September. In the 12 months through October, core PCE inflation is projected to have increased 3.3% after gaining 3.1% in the 12 months through September. These estimates could be impacted by producer price data for October that is due to be released on Friday.
"Inflation isn't dead; it is very much alive and the cost-of-living crisis rages on," said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS.

WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. inflation was higher than expected last month as the rising prices that powered sweeping Democratic victories in last week’s midterm elections appear likely to pose ongoing challenges for the White House and the Federal Reserve.
The consumer price index rose 0.4% from September to October, the Labor Department said Tuesday, down from 0.6% the previous month. The government did not report a yearly inflation rate because last year’s government shutdown meant no data was released for October 2025.
But excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 0.3%, the same as the preceding month. Both figures were a tenth of a point higher than forecast, and at an annual rate would be well above the Fed’s 2% target.
The new inflation data heightened concerns that strong consumer and business spending, combined with higher gas prices and supply disruptions stemming from tariffs and global turmoil, are creating increasingly stubborn inflation that could extend beyond temporary spikes in prices at the gas pump. The economy expanded at a 3.4% annual rate in the July-September quarter, mostly driven by consumer spending.
“It’s worrisome. There is a sense that inflation is broad, persistent, a little bit everywhere,” said Riccardo Trezzi, founder of Underlying Inflation, a consulting firm, and a former Fed economist. “The Fed should be very worried.”
Using rough estimates for last October’s data, Trezzi calculates that consumer prices rose 4% in October from a year ago, up from 3.7% in September. Core prices rose 2.8%, he estimates, up from 2.6%.
Americans’ struggles with high prices were evident as they ousted Republican majorities from the House and Senate last week. With historic gains in both chambers, Democrats in Congress will soon face the same challenges. President Donald Trump has acknowledged voter anger over the Iran war and gas prices but has shown no sign yet of changing course.
The AP Voter Poll, a survey of 100,000 voters, found about two-thirds blamed Trump’s policies for higher costs. About 9 in 10 said the cost of living was a “crucial” or “major” factor in their vote.
Federal Reserve may become more aggressive about raising borrowing costs
The persistence of elevated inflation makes it highly likely that the Fed will raise its key interest rate at its next meeting in December. It kept rates unchanged late last month, after raising them in September. The Fed increases borrowing costs in an effort to cool spending and bring down inflation.
Earlier Tuesday, Fed governor Christopher Waller, an outspoken member of the central bank’s rate-setting committee, said that a hike of a half-point next month was possible, double the size of the usual quarter-point increase.
“Economic activity is strong, the labor market is stable, but inflation is too high, well above” the Fed’s 2% goal, Waller said.
Stock prices fell in early trading Tuesday, and Treasury yields rose, on expectations of more persistent inflation and higher rates from the Fed.
Higher gas prices may have begun to spread through economy
Gas prices rose 1% from September to October, the government said, a stiff increase but still much lower than in previous months. Gas prices have soared more than 37% from a year ago. Still, oil prices have fallen sharply in recent days on hopes that the Iran conflict is fading, and gas costs have declined this month.
Yet there are signs higher energy prices are spreading into other parts of the economy, with air fares, public transportation, and delivery services all jumping in price. Electricity prices rose 0.9% from September to October, the most since April, and grocery prices jumped 0.4%, a painful rise after years of increases.
Beef prices rose 0.9% last month, after jumping nearly 14% in the first half of this year. Restaurant prices rose 0.5% from September to October, the most since January 2024. Rising shipping prices, driven up by more expensive gas, have lifted costs for restaurants and grocery stores, which may be passing them on to consumers.
Inflation has also been worsened by the massive investments flowing into artificial intelligence, which has contributed to higher prices for computer chips, electricity and consumer electronics. Voters swept dozens of candidates into office who had pledged to slow data center construction.
Computer prices jumped 0.5% last month, the government report showed, after rising nearly 10% in the year ending in September, lifted by more expensive chips. The cost of computers had been retreating for years as semiconductor chips became more efficient. That trend reversed course this year as prices rose sharply.
Prices are rising, and it’s not just gasoline
Prices are also rising in some sectors that have little to do with oil and gas or AI. Streaming video services have recently gotten more expensive, with Disney raising prices last month for its ad-supported Disney+ and Hulu streaming bundle to $12.49 a month from $11.99. The ad-free version rose by $2.50 to $21.49.
Prices also increased last month for an Apple TV/Peacock streaming bundle, to $17.99 from $14.99 a month.
Small businesses are bracing for a spending pullback by customers.
Chris Butler, CEO of National Tree Company, an artificial tree importer and wholesaler, says most of his customers now spend $200 or less on a tree. That is a big departure from the pandemic days when many people, flush with cash, were spending $300 to $400, he said.
“Inflation continues to persist,” he said. “Gas prices continue to be high, so consumers are hurting from a discretionary perspective.”
Last year, National Tree was forced to raise prices on its products, sourced in China and Cambodia, between 10% and 15% because of Trump’s tariffs, Butler said. Tariffs have come down, but now the firm is grappling with higher diesel costs.
Butler said the company, based in Cranford, N.J., doesn’t plan to raise prices again this year given the existing financial stress on customers, who are already spending less on trees.
Outside of inflation, other measures show the economy is largely doing well. The unemployment rate is a low 4.1% and growth is steady. Still, high prices have left most Americans with a dour view of the economy.
“It might not be a recession, but if you’re still living paycheck to paycheck and watching gas prices go up, grocery prices go up, your rent costs go up, it’s not going to feel like a robust economy,” said Jim Baird, chief investment officer at Plante Moran Financial Advisors.

By Paul Goldberg — Senior Correspondent | LGBT Business Finance News
NEW YORK, NY — (November 10, 2026) — Wall Street came under renewed selling pressure Tuesday after a hotter-than-expected October inflation report rattled financial markets, pushed U.S. Treasury yields toward the psychologically significant 5% threshold, and intensified concerns that the Federal Reserve could deliver another interest rate increase before the end of 2026.
The latest inflation figures disrupted investor confidence following Monday’s powerful stock market rebound, placing the Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500, and technology-heavy Nasdaq Composite back under pressure as traders reassessed the direction of U.S. monetary policy.

• Federal Workers Take Trump Healthcare Ban to Court as 2027 Benefits Deadline Looms
• Wall Street’s AI Bubble Warning: Democratic Sweep Triggers $2.5 Trillion Nasdaq Meltdown

• Exxon, Chevron Cash In as $130 Billion Oil Boom Threatens Trump’s Midterms
• Get the Latest in LGBT Business Finance News on JRL CHARTS
For investors already navigating volatility across artificial intelligence, technology stocks, and the broader economy, Tuesday’s inflation surprise introduced another significant obstacle to a sustained Wall Street recovery.
October Inflation Exceeds Wall Street Forecasts
According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Consumer Price Index increased 0.4% in October, exceeding economists’ expectations of a 0.3% monthly increase.
Although the figure represented a slowdown from September’s 0.6% advance, the higher-than-anticipated reading reinforced concerns that inflationary pressures remain deeply embedded in the American economy.
Core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, increased 0.3%, compared with economists’ forecasts of 0.2%.
The report also revealed continued pressure on household expenses:
• Shelter costs: Increased 0.3%, accounting for more than 30% of the overall monthly CPI increase.
• Food prices: Climbed 0.5%, including increases in grocery and restaurant prices.
• Energy prices: Advanced 0.7%, following September’s much sharper increase.
The figures highlight the continuing challenge facing the Federal Reserve as policymakers attempt to bring inflation closer to their long-term 2% objective without destabilizing economic growth.
Federal Reserve Rate-Hike Fears Return
The inflation surprise immediately shifted attention toward the Federal Reserve’s December monetary policy meeting.
Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller has signaled that persistent inflation could justify a more aggressive policy response, including consideration of a 50-basis-point interest rate increase.
Such a move would represent a larger adjustment than the conventional quarter-percentage-point increase and could place additional pressure on businesses, consumers, and financial markets.
Investors are increasingly concerned that the central bank may need to maintain restrictive monetary conditions longer than previously anticipated.
Higher interest rates typically increase borrowing costs, discourage corporate investment, and reduce the relative attractiveness of equities, particularly growth-oriented technology stocks whose valuations depend heavily on expectations of future earnings.
The latest inflation report has therefore transformed December’s Federal Reserve meeting into a critical event for Wall Street’s year-end outlook.
Treasury Yields Surge as Bond Markets React
The U.S. Treasury market delivered one of Tuesday’s clearest warning signals.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield climbed toward 4.99%, approaching the closely watched 5% level, while the policy-sensitive two-year Treasury yield jumped approximately 19 basis points to around 4.73%–4.75%.
These movements reflect expectations that interest rates could remain elevated or increase further.
Rising Treasury yields have important consequences beyond Wall Street.
They can influence mortgage rates, corporate financing expenses, commercial lending, and the cost of servicing government debt.
For publicly traded companies, higher borrowing costs can constrain expansion plans and reduce future profitability. For consumers, tighter financial conditions can make purchasing homes, financing vehicles, and carrying credit card balances increasingly expensive.
The bond-market reaction underscores how a single inflation report can rapidly alter expectations across the entire financial system.
Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq Retreat After Monday’s Rally
Major U.S. stock indexes moved lower during Tuesday’s trading session, surrendering part of the previous day’s gains.
Early market reports indicated:
• Dow Jones Industrial Average: Declined roughly 0.5%–0.6%, with losses fluctuating throughout the session.
• S&P 500: Fell approximately 0.7%.
• Nasdaq Composite: Dropped roughly 0.8%–1%, reflecting renewed pressure on technology and growth stocks.
These figures reflect intraday market movements, not final closing results.
The downturn followed Monday’s strong rebound, illustrating how quickly investor sentiment can reverse when inflation and interest-rate expectations change.
Technology companies remain particularly vulnerable to rising bond yields because higher discount rates can reduce the present value investors assign to anticipated future profits.
AI and Technology Stocks Face Another Test
Tuesday’s inflation-driven decline comes amid broader uncertainty surrounding technology valuations and the sustainability of the artificial intelligence investment boom.
Wall Street has already experienced sharp fluctuations as investors reassess the enormous capital expenditures associated with AI infrastructure, data centers, semiconductor manufacturing, and next-generation computing systems.
The combination of elevated valuations and renewed interest-rate concerns creates a challenging environment for companies whose market prices depend on ambitious long-term growth expectations.
Although the inflation report is not directly connected to the underlying performance of AI companies, tighter monetary conditions can amplify existing market volatility.

The consequences of persistent inflation extend well beyond the stock market.
Small businesses, independent retailers, manufacturers, and service providers face a difficult operating environment when borrowing costs remain elevated and household purchasing power comes under pressure.
Higher financing expenses can discourage inventory expansion, equipment purchases, commercial real estate investment, and new hiring.
For specialty retailers and distributors, the combination of increased operating costs and cautious consumer spending can also complicate inventory management and long-term planning.
These pressures are particularly relevant to independent businesses competing against larger corporations with greater access to capital.
A prolonged period of restrictive monetary policy could therefore create additional challenges for entrepreneurs and business owners heading into 2027.
Wall Street’s Next Challenge: Inflation, Interest Rates and Investor Confidence
The immediate question facing financial markets is whether October’s inflation surprise will force the Federal Reserve to pursue a more aggressive interest-rate strategy.
Investors will closely monitor additional economic releases, Treasury yield movements, and comments from Federal Reserve officials for indications of how policymakers intend to respond.
The upcoming Producer Price Index report will provide another measure of inflationary pressures within the economy.

sources.news_title: US inflation slows less than expected, lifting rate hike odds
sources.text:
US inflation data released Tuesday slowed slightly in October but still overshot analyst estimates, raising expectations for further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes.
The consumer price index for October rose 0.4 percent from September, down from the prior month's 0.6 percent increase, according to Labor Department data. Analysts had projected a 0.3 percent increase.
The improvement from the prior month reflected a significant moderation in energy price increases from September. The prior CPI report had shown the effects of a big jump in fuel prices following renewed clashes in the US-Iran war over the summer.
But food prices shot higher in October, along with medical care, household furnishings and several other categories.
The report follows last week's US midterm elections in which voters turned sharply against President Donald Trump's Republican Party in part due to persistent inflation.
The Labor Department was unable to translate the figures into a year-over-year number because there was no report in October 2025 due to a government shutdown. But the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland estimated the jump as 3.8 percent, well above the Fed's two percent target.
The report "sets the stage for a December Fed hike," read the headline on a note from Oxford Economics.
"Though energy prices moderated as expected, it was food inflation that drove the forecast miss of last month's headline CPI," Oxford Economics said in the note.
"Grocery-store inflation accelerated notably after a string of quiescent readings, underscoring the lags between energy price shocks and nonenergy consumer prices."
Price hikes for energy slowed significantly compared with the prior report, with the gasoline index rising one percent -- far below the 9.1 percent spike in September from August.
The index for food rose 0.5 percent in October after being unchanged in September.
- 'Supersize' rate hike? -
Joseph Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM, said the inflation report could keep a "supersize hike on the table at the December Fed meeting," alluding to comments earlier Tuesday from Fed Governor Christopher Waller.
"In my estimation this requires rate hikes by the Fed and we think that a December rate hike is baked in the cake given that this is the final CPI report that the Fed will get to observe," Brusuelas said.
Futures markets now see a December rate hike as essentially guaranteed, with 85 percent of trader bets expecting a one-quarter percentage point hike and 15 predicting a half-percentage point increase.
Earlier Tuesday, Waller signaled support for a December rate increase due to persistently elevated inflation, saying the central bank must act "sooner rather than later, to return inflation to a path that will reach two percent in the medium term."
Waller cited inflationary effects from the artificial intelligence buildout and pointed to Fed research that suggests "energy price pressures may pass through to goods and services in a more sustained way than in the past."
Speaking a few hours before the CPI release, Waller said he was "leaning towards" a 25 basis point rate hike in December even with an October report showing moderation in pricing pressures.
But if October pricing dynamics are similar to last month's, "then a stronger policy move may be needed," he said.
"In that case, I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting," Waller added. "Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take."
Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan also strongly endorsed additional rate hikes, citing the data as she urged "prompt" action before persistent inflation "becomes baked into behavior," she said in a speech late Tuesday morning.
Logan estimated that the Fed funds rate must rise by "at least 50 basis points" in order "to bring the inflation trend back to target," she said.
Logan acknowledged that energy prices have played a role, but described inflationary trends as "broader than that," noting that higher prices in categories like visiting the doctor or dining out "aren't particularly sensitive to tariffs, conflict in the Middle East or surging demand for computer chips."
"It remains clear to me, given the current outlook, that the FOMC needs to implement at least two more 25-basis-point rate increases," Logan said.

sources.text:
US petrol prices are down, but elevated inflation continues
Inflation remained high, despite some easing in fuel prices caused by the US war on Iran.
Consumer prices in the United States increased in October more than expected, even as petrol prices fell to a four-month low after some easing of concerns about the long-term impact of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz on global markets.
In its latest report released on Tuesday, the US Department of Labor’s Bureau of Labor Statistics said the Consumer Price Index (CPI) for all items rose by 0.4 percent in October, continuing an inflationary trend since July. The average cost of shelter, as well as food, also rose in October, according to the agency.
The Labor Department’s report was higher than the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, which had forecast the CPI to increase by 0.2 percent, and economists polled by FactSet, who had predicted an increase of 0.3 percent, despite the lowering pressure on energy prices.
On Monday, US President Donald Trump said that future military action against Tehran was unlikely. “Iran militarily is effectively over,” Trump said. “We’re just keeping it the status quo, and we’re doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbours.”
The average price of a gallon of petrol fell below $4 ($1.06 per litre) for the first time since July, according to the American Automobile Association. But the average price, currently $3.98, is still significantly higher than the $3.07 mark it was at a year ago. The average price of a gallon of petrol was $2.98 ($0.78 per litre) on February 28, when the US and Israel first struck Iran.
The economy and cost-of-living concerns were leading concerns for voters in midterm elections that were held on November 3, which saw Republicans lose control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released on the eve of the elections found that 78 percent of voters said cost-of-living was very important or the most important issue for them when considering how they would vote. Democrats, the poll found, were favoured by 43 percent of voters, compared with 32 percent who preferred Republicans to handle it.
How voters view Trump himself has also turned largely negative since the war and its impact on the economy. Only 32 percent of voters approved of his job performance, according to the Reuters/Ipsos poll, just one point above his record low of 31 percent last month.
Trump’s Republican Party was dealt major losses in the midterm elections, losing typically Republican seats in Congress in states like Texas and Kansas.
Trump himself, as well as key members of his administration like Vice President JD Vance, have acknowledged that the war on Iran played a part in those electoral losses.

Early promise fades after hot US inflation print
The FTSE 100 has closed lower in London as early advances evaporated in the wake of another strong US inflation print.
The FTSE 100 index closed down 31.28 points, 0.3%, at 10,751.59. It had earlier traded as high as 10,868.51.
The FTSE 250 ended 40.31 points higher, 0.2%, at 24,746.65, and the AIM all-share shed 1.85 points, 0.2%, at 759.54.
In Europe, the CAC 40 in Paris rose 0.6%, while the DAX 40 in Frankfurt climbed 0.3%.
In the US, equity markets were lower. Around the time of the London equities close on Tuesday, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 0.6%, the S&P 500 was 0.7% lower, while the Nasdaq Composite gave back 1.0%.
In the US, figures released by the Bureau of Labour Statistics showed US consumer prices rose more than expected in October, as higher food, housing and energy costs continued to put pressure on households.
The consumer price index rose by 0.4% month-on-month in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, slowing from a 0.6% increase in September but exceeding the FXStreet-cited consensus forecast of 0.3%.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, remained steady at 0.3% month-on-month, matching the increases recorded in September and August but coming in above expectations of 0.2%.
Leslie Preston, senior economist at TD Economics, said inflation pressures were fairly broad-based across categories, and “most importantly” show little sign of cooling.
“The source of inflation pressure has shifted from tariffs to higher energy costs and strong demand for tech-related goods due to the AI boom. Where it hasn’t shifted is lower,” Ms Preston added.
Barclays analyst Pooja Sriram noted it was the third consecutive upside surprise in core CPI, which “reinforces the message that underlying price pressures remain firm” and “strongly supports” a December Federal Open Market Committee rate hike.
Analysts at Morgan Stanley agreed.
“For the Fed, the report increases the likelihood of a more hawkish path. We expect energy pass-through to put further upward pressure on core goods prices over the next few months, with potentially a sharper acceleration in 1Q27 as firms reset prices at the start of the calendar year. If firmer core goods inflation is accompanied by continued acceleration in services, as we have seen in the past two prints, the Fed may need to do more than we currently expect. We expect two 25bp hikes, in December and March.”
Read More
Ahead of the figures, US Federal Reserve governor Chris Waller said he would support a rate hike in December and warned that if inflation continued to accelerate he would support a half-percentage-point increase to protect the central bank’s credibility.
The data lit up the dollar and saw yields on US Treasuries tick upwards.
The pound was quoted at 1.3323 dollars late Tuesday afternoon, down from 1.3415 dollars at the same time on Monday. Against the euro, sterling declined to 1.1949 euros from 1.1974 euros.

Investors will be hoping the upcoming initial public offering from Anthropic will give the market a lift.
On Tuesday, Anthropic said it could raise between 84.6 billion dollars to 93.7 billion dollars through the IPO, which could value the business at around one trillion dollars.
In a filing on Tuesday, San Francisco-based Claude chatbot maker Anthropic said it plans to sell 801.4 million shares, with a further 23.6 million shares being sold by other shareholders.
Should the underwriters sell more than 825 million shares of Class A common stock, they have the option to purchase up to an additional 123.8 million shares from Anthropic, the statement said.
Anthropic currently expects that the initial public offering price per share will be between 70.00 dollars and 78.00 dollars. This could value Anthropic at 1.02 trillion dollars, based on the shares outstanding listed in the filing.
In London, equity markets had earlier pushed higher, reflecting a further fall in the oil price as hopes grow of a peaceful resolution to the US-Iran war.
US secretary of state Marco Rubio on Tuesday said he saw no need to resume major combat operations against Iran because economic sanctions and other restrictions were working so effectively.
“The economic campaign (against Iran) is so devastating that right now there is no need for major combat operations,” Mr Rubio said after a meeting of G7 foreign ministers in Paris. “That’s what I told our allies here today.”
Brent oil was trading at 91.74 dollars a barrel on Tuesday, lower than 94.27 dollars late Monday.
Reflecting the price move, oil majors BP and Shell fell 0.8% and 2.1% respectively in London.

Among smaller companies, EDX Medical Group jumped 19% after launching what it described as the first breast cancer prognostic test in the UK capable of assessing both short-term and long-term risks of recurrence, extending up to 15 years.
The Cambridge-based diagnostics company entered into an agreement with US-based Caris Life Sciences to supply its Caris MI Clarity test in the UK.

sources.news_title: Prices Rise 0.4% in October, Hotter Than Expected, as Fed Officials Open the Door to Bigger Hikes
sources.text:
Prices Rise 0.4% in October, Hotter Than Expected, as Fed Officials Open the Door to Bigger Hikes
Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, a tenth of a point more than economists expected, cementing expectations for a December interest rate hike and lifting the odds of a bigger one.
The Labor Department’s Bureau of Labor Statistics released the figures Tuesday, CNBC reported. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones had looked for 0.3%. Core prices, which strip out food and energy, rose 0.3% against a 0.2% forecast.
Headline inflation cooled from a 0.6% jump in September, while core prices matched September’s 0.3% pace.
The bureau did not publish a yearly inflation rate. Last year’s government shutdown kept it from collecting enough data in October 2025, leaving no comparison month.
Annual inflation had reached 3.7% in September, Reuters reported, as the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran pushed up oil prices on top of tariffs imposed last year.
Core prices rising 0.3% a month would translate into yearly inflation above 4% if sustained, Reuters noted. The Fed’s target is 2%.
Groceries, Gas and Rent
The details showed price pressure well beyond the gas station. Gasoline rose 1% and energy 0.7% for the month, even as pump prices have fallen in recent weeks, CNBC reported.
Food costs climbed 0.5%. Beef rose 0.9% and snacks 1%, while transportation services jumped 0.8%.
Shelter rose 0.3% and accounted for more than 30% of the overall increase. Used car and truck prices were the main bright spot, falling 1.2%.
“This was the report the market could least afford to see,” Karen Manna, fixed income investment strategist at Federated Hermes, told CNBC.
Bond investors agreed. The 10-year Treasury yield, the benchmark for mortgages, car loans and credit cards, briefly traded above 5% before settling near 4.99%, CNBC reported. The 2-year yield surged more than 18 basis points to about 4.74%.
Stocks gave back part of Monday’s rally. The S&P 500 fell 0.38% to 7,521.48, the Nasdaq slid 0.74% and the Dow lost 161.95 points to 52,227.80, according to preliminary closing figures reported by CNA.
Fed Governor Christopher Waller had said in London before the release that a core reading around 0.3% would make him consider a half-point hike at the Fed’s Dec. 8-9 meeting.
“Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk,” Waller said, according to the same CNBC report.
Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan went further at an energy conference in Houston.
“It remains clear to me, given the current outlook, that the FOMC needs to implement at least two more 25-basis-point rate increases,” she said in her prepared remarks.
“It may be possible to move more rapidly this winter than the FOMC has moved so far this fall,” Logan added.
She called the current 3.75% to 4% policy rate too low and said it was “adding to inflationary pressures,” Reuters reported.
Futures markets now see a quarter-point December hike as nearly certain. The odds of a half-point move rose to about 15% in the morning before easing to roughly 10% late in the day, according to Reuters.

sources.text:
On Tuesday, a newly released batch of worse-than-forecasted data prompted a host at Fox News to declare that President Donald Trump’s economy is performing “nowhere near good enough” to prevent the Federal Reserve from taking dramatic measures in hopes of correcting the situation. What’s more, according to Big Money Show host Taylor Riggs, persistently high inflation may not only prompt the Fed to raise interest rates, but they may shoot up higher than expected, with major impacts for consumers.
Riggs was responding to the Consumer Price Index data for October that was released Tuesday morning, which revealed that “headline” inflation – the rate of inflation across all consumer sectors – remains elevated beyond expectations, climbing by 0.4 percent in October from a month earlier, higher than the 0.3 percent economists were hoping for. The report also revealed that "core" inflation – which strips out volatile food and energy prices – rose 0.3 percent, coming in ahead of the 0.2 percent economists were expecting to match September's level. Overall, the hardest hit sectors include vital expenses like food, rent, medical care, and transportation. As Riggs notes, while the speed of the inflation increase has decelerated slightly, “it is hotter than expected. Similar to the core, flat in line with where we were before, but again, hotter than expected. We were looking at maybe a deceleration here because we thought a big jump in gas prices would start to come down. And I would say that we are nowhere near good enough.”
She went on to remind that earlier in the morning, Federal Reserve Board of Governors member Christopher Waller had warned that if core came in at 0.3 percent or higher – “which is where we are” – he would want a 50 basis point hike rather than a more modest 25 basis point hike. "Inflation is too high … this means that even if, as I expect, the monthly rate of inflation improves in October, I am leaning toward supporting an increase in our policy rate of 25 basis points at the FOMC's December meeting," Waller said in a speech in London. But if the October inflation data came out higher than expected – as it has – then more dramatic action may be necessary, Waller said. "In that case, I believe a 50-basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting," he explained. "Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take." He also noted, “Let's just say it: September's inflation data were bad. There was no silver lining.”
While raising federal interest rates can help tame inflation, it also comes with downsides. As it climbs, so do mortgage rates in an already unaffordable housing market, and so do borrowing rates for businesses, which can restrict growth, hiring, and other investments. "One hopes inflation starts returning to normal, but that's a hope right now, not a reality," economist Justin Wolfers posted in response to the latest data.

sources.news_title: US inflation runs hotter than expected as higher prices extend beyond gas station
sources.text:
US inflation runs hotter than expected as higher prices extend beyond gas station
Summary
U.S. consumer prices rose 0.4 percent from September to October, the Labor Department said Tuesday in Washington, as price increases extended beyond gasoline. Core prices, excluding food and energy, rose 0.3 percent, and both monthly increases were a tenth of a point above forecasts. The report heightened concerns about persistent inflation and the possibility of a Federal Reserve rate increase in December. Higher costs were reported across energy, food, transportation, computers and streaming services.
Key Facts
- The government did not report an annual inflation rate because the 2025 government shutdown meant no October data were released last year.
- Riccardo Trezzi estimated that consumer prices rose 4 percent year over year in October and core prices rose 2.8 percent, using rough estimates for the missing October 2025 data.
- Gas prices increased 1 percent from September to October and were more than 37 percent higher than a year earlier.
- Electricity prices rose 0.9 percent month over month, grocery prices rose 0.4 percent, and restaurant prices rose 0.5 percent.
- Computer prices increased 0.5 percent in October after rising nearly 10 percent in the year through September.
WASHINGTON — U.S. inflation was higher than expected last month as the rising prices that powered sweeping Democratic victories in last week’s midterm elections appear likely to pose ongoing challenges for the White House and the Federal Reserve.
The consumer price index rose 0.4 percent from September to October, the Labor Department said Tuesday, down from 0.6 percent the previous month. The government did not report a yearly inflation rate because last year's government shutdown meant no data was released for October 2025.
But excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 0.3 percent, the same as the preceding month. Both figures were a tenth of a point higher than forecast, and at an annual rate would be well above the Fed's 2 percent target.
The new inflation data heightened concerns that strong consumer and business spending, combined with higher gas prices and supply disruptions stemming from tariffs and global turmoil, are creating increasingly stubborn inflation that could extend beyond temporary spikes in prices at the gas pump. The economy expanded at a 3.4 percent annual rate in the July-September quarter, mostly driven by consumer spending.
“It's worrisome. There is a sense that inflation is broad, persistent, a little bit everywhere,” said Riccardo Trezzi, founder of Underlying Inflation, a consulting firm, and a former Fed economist. “The Fed should be very worried.”
Using rough estimates for last October's data, Trezzi calculates that consumer prices rose 4 percent in October from a year ago, up from 3.7 percent in September. Core prices rose 2.8 percent, he estimates, up from 2.6 percent.
Americans’ struggles with high prices were evident as they ousted Republican majorities from the House and Senate last week. With historic gains in both chambers, Democrats in Congress will soon face the same challenges. President Donald Trump has acknowledged voter anger over the Iran war and gas prices but has shown no sign yet of changing course.
The AP Voter Poll, a survey of 100,000 voters, found about two-thirds blamed Trump’s policies for higher costs. About 9 in 10 said the cost of living was a “crucial” or “major” factor in their vote.
Federal Reserve may become more aggressive about raising borrowing costs
The persistence of elevated inflation makes it highly likely that the Fed will raise its key interest rate at its next meeting in December. The consumer price index rose 0.4 per cent last month after advancing 0.6 per cent in September, the Labor Department’s Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said on Tuesday (Nov 10). Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the CPI climbing 0.3 per cent over the month.
The BLS did not publish year-on-year inflation readings because last year’s federal government shutdown prevented the collection of consumer price data in October 2025, leaving no comparison base.
Annual consumer inflation jumped 3.7 per cent in September.
Inflation is running well above the US central bank’s 2 per cent target. The US-Israeli war with Iran has boosted oil prices, combining with the import tariffs implemented by the Trump administration last year to lift the cost of living.
High inflation contributed to the heavy losses suffered by President Donald Trump’s Republican Party in the midterm elections last week.
Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the CPI increased 0.3 per cent last month after gaining 0.3 per cent in September. The so-called core CPI was forecast to have climbed 0.2 per cent in October.
The missing data from last year has no impact on the calculation of the personal consumption expenditures price index readings that are tracked by the Fed to gauge progress towards its inflation target. Both measures are running above 3 per cent.
Odds that the Fed may raise interest rates by half a percentage point at its December meeting jumped, as October’s inflation cleared the bar set by one key policymaker for considering a quicker pace of rate hikes.
The Fed last month left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the range of 3.75 to 4 per cent.
In comments overnight in London, Fed governor Christopher Waller said that a core reading of 0.3 per cent for October would prompt him to consider a half point hike at the Fed’s meeting from Dec 8 to 9.
With a quarter-point rate hike all but assured, market bets on a larger increase were rapidly building amid a broad bond market sell-off and at mid-morning were close to 15 per cent.

Food prices climbed 0.5%, including a 0.4% increase in grocery prices and a 0.5% increase in the cost of dining out.
Energy prices increased 0.7%, considerably slower than September’s 5.2% surge. However, gasoline prices rose another 1% during October after climbing 9.1% the previous month.
Gasoline prices were 37.4% higher than a year earlier, reflecting substantial increases in fuel costs amid disruptions associated with the war involving Iran.
Electricity prices increased 0.9% in October, while fuel oil rose 2%.
Other categories also experienced price increases. Medical care costs rose 0.3%, including a 0.8% increase in hospital services and a 0.4% rise in physicians’ services.
Motor vehicle insurance increased 0.7%, while education costs climbed 0.3% and new vehicle prices rose 0.2%.
Some categories provided limited relief. Used car and truck prices declined 1.2%, while communication costs edged down 0.1%.
The October report differs from typical inflation releases because the Labor Department did not publish an overall annual inflation rate.
A federal government shutdown prevented the collection of consumer price data in October 2025, leaving the agency without the information necessary to calculate standard year-over-year comparisons for most categories.
The annual inflation rate reached 3.7% in September, well above the Federal Reserve’s 2% inflation target.
According to Reuters’ Nov. 10 analysis, the latest figures reinforced expectations that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates at its December meeting.
The central bank held its benchmark interest rate at 3.75% to 4% in October, maintaining its restrictive policy stance as officials evaluated inflation and employment conditions.
Financial markets have increasingly anticipated a quarter-percentage-point rate increase in December, although policymakers have not announced a decision.
Federal Reserve officials must balance inflation concerns against the potential economic consequences of higher borrowing costs.
An increase in the benchmark rate can make mortgages, auto loans, credit cards and business financing more expensive, potentially slowing consumer spending and economic activity.
However, higher interest rates can also help reduce inflation by limiting demand.
The October inflation report arrives as the economy continues absorbing higher energy costs and changes in federal trade policy.
The military conflict involving Iran has disrupted energy markets, while tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump’s administration have increased costs for some imported products.
Economists have warned that businesses facing higher transportation, energy and import expenses may pass some of those costs to consumers.
The effects vary across industries, making it difficult to attribute individual price increases to a single policy or economic development.
October’s figures nevertheless indicate that inflation remains a challenge for American households.
The food index’s 0.5% monthly increase was its largest since April, while shelter costs continued rising despite previous signs of moderation.
Higher prices for groceries, insurance, medical services and utilities can place particular pressure on households whose incomes have not kept pace with expenses.
The Labor Department separately reported that inflation-adjusted average hourly earnings were unchanged in October, indicating that wage increases did not produce an overall improvement in purchasing power during the month.
That finding highlights the difference between nominal wage growth and the amount of goods and services workers can purchase with their earnings.
Although the pace of overall price increases slowed from September, the October report does not indicate that consumer prices are falling. Instead, it shows that prices continued rising at a somewhat slower monthly rate.
The latest inflation figures also come shortly after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when economic concerns, including the cost of living, featured prominently in congressional campaigns.
The Federal Reserve is scheduled to meet again in December, when policymakers will consider the inflation report alongside employment figures and other economic indicators.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics will release its November consumer price report on Dec. 10, providing another assessment of inflation after the Fed’s scheduled policy meeting.
For now, October’s higher-than-expected increase reinforces concerns that consumer prices remain under pressure, with housing, food and energy expenses continuing to affect household budgets and complicate the Federal Reserve’s efforts to bring inflation under control.

sources.news_title: Inflation hotter than expected in October — adding to Fed’s case for rate hike
sources.text:
Inflation hotter than expected in October as energy, food prices surge
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Inflation came in hotter than expected in October as energy and food prices continued to surge – setting up the Federal Reserve to hike interest rates next month and fueling fears of more hikes down the line.
The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% over the month – slowing from a 0.6% monthly pace in September but hotter than estimates of a 0.3% rise, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said Tuesday. The 12-month inflation rate was not released due to the government shutdown last fall, which halted data collection.
On a core basis, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, the CPI rose 0.3% in October – the same monthly pace as September and August, and higher than estimates of a 0.2% increase.
Traders bet on a more than 90% chance rates will be raised by a quarter-point to the 4% to 4.25% range at the Fed’s Dec. 9 meeting – and roughly 10% odds rates will be hiked by a half-point, according to CME FedWatch.
Speaking in London just hours before the CPI report, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he’s leaning toward a quarter-point hike at next month’s meeting. He said if the data swayed him at all, it would be toward a larger hike – not a hold.
If core inflation rose 0.3% or more – as the data showed it did in October – the Fed should consider a half-point hike, he added.
Following the report, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said officials may need to pick up the pace of increases “this winter [more rapidly] than the FOMC has moved so far this fall.”
Recent jobs data showed hiring was surprisingly strong in October and the unemployment rate fell, adding to the case for a rate hike as the Fed can remain squarely focused on inflation.
Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management, said the question is no longer whether the Fed will raise rates in December – but whether they’ll immediately follow it up with another hike in January, “which would have been unexpected before today.”
Alternatively, the Fed might “take their time and raise rates slowly next year,” he said in a note Tuesday. “All of this matters for markets, because a more patient Fed would be easier for stock bulls to navigate, while a more aggressive Fed could prove to be too big of a headwind for the market to overcome next year.”
By about 3:35 p.m. ET, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 180 points, or 0.3%, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq slid 0.5% and 0.9%, respectively.
The US 30-year Treasury yield ticked higher to 5.351% while the 10-year yield hit 4.988%, nearing 5% again. The dollar extended gains against major global currencies.
October’s inflation data showed price increases are still weighing heavily on consumers’ purchasing power. Average weekly earnings for workers in October were flat over the month when adjusted for inflation, according to a New York Times estimate.
It’s the seventh straight month of price increases outpacing wage gains, which could help explain why consumer sentiment has remained low and Democrats swept congressional midterm elections across the country.
Despite stubborn inflation, consumer spending has remained strong – but Americans have increasingly been falling into debt, according to data the New York Fed released Tuesday.
Credit card balances hit a record $1.29 trillion in the third quarter and total household debt – including mortgages, auto loans and student loans – reached a record $19.1 trillion.
Over the past three months, prices have risen at a roughly 5.7% annualized pace, according to the Wall Street Journal – far above the Fed’s 2% inflation goal.
Food prices were one of the largest drivers of inflation in October, rising 0.5% in October. Rising diesel costs likely bled into farmers’ costs, as tractors and other equipment typically run on the pricey fuel. El Niño weather conditions have also slammed crops.
Energy costs also continued to rise as the Strait of Hormuz crisis has blocked off crucial shipments. Gasoline jumped 1% over the month and 37.4% over the past 12 months. Fuel oil – which is used to heat homes – also saw one of the largest increases over the month, setting off alarms just ahead of the winter season.
Toys – a heavily tariff-sensitive category – jumped about 1% over the month and are higher over the year, which could be an especially painful point for shoppers headed into the holiday season.
Computer prices rose roughly 11.8% over the past 12 months, while software soared nearly 26% as shortages have sent prices surging amid the nationwide data-center buildout.
Airfares rose 0.4% in October and about 27.8% over the year. It’s one of the categories most impacted by rising energy prices, as fuel accounts for the bulk of airlines’ operating costs.
Shelter prices rose 0.3% over the month and apparel ticked up 0.1%. Appliances also increased 0.5%.
Used cars and trucks provided some rare relief to consumers, falling 1.2% over the month and 3.3% over the past 12 months. It was also one of the few categories with an annual inflation rate, since the data is based on real prices, not surveys.
National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett called the inflation report “disappointing” during a brief appearance on Fox Business’ “Varney & Co.” Tuesday morning. As of publication, President Trump has not yet reacted to the data.

sources.news_title: Inflation report finds prices rose faster than expected before midterms
sources.text:
Price increases did not slow as much as was anticipated in October, according to the latest inflation report from the Department of Labor, with energy and several other consumer costs continuing to drive elevated inflation ahead of the midterm elections.
According to Tuesday’s report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), consumer prices rose 0.4 percent in October. Ahead of the release, the consensus among analysts had been only a 0.3 percent increase in the Consumer Price Index (CPI).
The latest report follows a fuel-driven 0.6 percent gain in September.
Read More
First Assessment Since the Midterms
Missing from the report is the annual rate. The government shutdown which took place last year interrupted the agency’s data gathering efforts, meaning it had no October report to use for comparison for the 12-month rate.
Stripping out food and energy, core inflation hit 0.3 percent in October, in line with September but slightly faster than the 0.2 percent forecasts.
Tuesday’s report was the first comprehensive look at consumer prices since the midterms, in which Democrats won both the House and Senate in large part due to inflationary concerns and the rising cost of living.
And the report was also significant in its implications for monetary policy and the Federal Reserve’s rate outlook. The central bank kept interest rates steady in late October following a quarter-point hike in September, with analysts now parsing economic data and policymaker remarks for hints as to its calculus going into December's meeting.
“Markets are benefiting from an improvement in the geopolitical outlook, but the underlying macroeconomic and corporate risks remain unresolved. Lower energy prices could help ease inflation expectations, but the Fed will need evidence of broader disinflation before reconsidering its policy stance,” Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at Capital.com, wrote in a note shared ahead of the release.
The inflation data follows a better-than-expected jobs report from the BLS, which revealed that the economy added 165,000 roles in October compared with a consensus forecast of only 65,000.
“The key question is whether today's inflation figures support the recovery or remind investors that resilient economic growth and persistent price pressures could keep borrowing costs elevated for longer,” Hathorn wrote.
Rising Energy Costs
According to the BLS, some of the largest increases were again in the energy category in October, which rose 0.7 percent. Gas was up 1 percent and fuel oil by 2 percent, while electricity rose 0.9 percent. Household piped gas was down 0.8 percent, however. While the BLS did not publish annual rates, it said that gasoline costs were up 37.4 percent between October 2025 and October 2026.
According to AAA, the national average for regular unleaded was $3.98 per gallon as of Tuesday—down from $4.37 a month ago but up from $3.07 this time last year.
Food rose 0.5 percent in October, according to the BLS, with food at home—groceries—rising 0.4 percent, and food away from home rising by 0.5 percent.
Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, said on X that the figures imply an annual rate of around 4 percent.
“There was a big jump in grocery prices,” she wrote. “Eating out, electricity, transportation (esp. airfares), rent and medical services (esp. hospitals) all seeing sizable monthly price increases.”
Is Another Rate Hike Coming?
The report is the last before the Federal Reserve’s final meeting of 2026, set to take place on December 8 and 9, at which members of the Federal Open Market Committee will vote on whether to change rates or hold these steady amid changing employment and inflation circumstances.
“[Fed Chair] Kevin Warsh keeps telling us the Fed will deliver on price stability, but we’re seeing scant evidence that inflation is heading in the right direction,” Tom Graff, chief investment officer of financial advisory firm Facet, wrote in a note on Tuesday.
However, some have said that the report shows progress despite the figures coming in hotter than predicted, and that this could bolster the case for the central bank holding off on another hike.
“Lingering tariff effects and higher energy prices account for much of the inflation overshoot,” Josh Hirt, Senior U.S. Economist at Vanguard, wrote in a note following the release. “Excluding those supply factors, underlying inflation is much closer to the Fed’s 2 percent target.”
Hirt said that the increase in core inflation reflected “three outsized shocks: tariffs, energy prices, and AI-related demand,” which are painting a worse picture of underlying inflation.
"Energy effects will take longer to fade. Oil prices have remained near $100 per barrel for much of the year, extending their contribution to inflation. But absent a renewed and sustained increase in prices, that contribution should remain limited."
The CME FedWatch tool, which gauges the odds of Fed actions based on 30-Day Fed Funds futures, shows that traders are banking on a hike come December. There is an 85 percent chance of a 25-basis-point rate increase, up from 77 percent last week, and now a 15 percent chance of a larger, 50-point increase in the target rate.
