sources.news_title: Inflation remained elevated in October, CPI report shows, upping odds of Fed interest rate hike
sources.text:
Inflation remained elevated in October, CPI report shows, upping odds of Fed interest rate hike
Consumer prices rose more than economists expected in October on a monthly basis, offering little relief to Americans grappling with high living costs.
The Consumer Price Index, which tracks changes in prices over time, rose at a monthly pace of 0.4%, the Labor Department reported on Tuesday.
The Labor Department did not report a year-over-year inflation rate for October 2026 because the 2025 government shutdown left it without October 2025 consumer price data for comparison.
By the numbers
October's monthly inflation increase cooled from September, when headline inflation rose 0.6% on a monthly basis.
However, the figure was hotter than expected, with economists polled by FactSet predicting October prices would rise 0.3% month-over-month.
The October inflation data is one of the first snapshots of the economy following the midterm elections, which underscored Americans' frustration with high prices.
"Today's CPI report suggests underlying inflation remains more persistent than the Fed would like," Andrew Davis, head of investment strategy at Bryn Mawr Trust, said in an email. "While headline inflation moderated from September, core prices rose 0.3% for the third consecutive month, indicating that underlying price pressures have yet to meaningfully ease."
While inflation in recent months has largely been driven by higher energy prices, October's data shows that costs for other types of goods and products are also rising. Shelter costs, which rose 0.3% in October, accounted for more than 30% of the monthly all-items increase, the Labor Department said.
Food prices also accelerated, rising at a monthly pace of 0.5% last month after remaining flat in September, the data shows.
Energy prices
Energy costs, which have surged due to the Iran war, contributed less to the monthly rise in inflation than in past reports. Energy prices rose 0.7% in October, compared to 5.2% in September.
Gas prices have been falling for weeks as stations switch to cheaper winter blend and people pull back from summer travel.
Global oil costs, the main factor in setting prices at the pump, have also dipped amid hopes that the midterm elections could open the door to a deal between the U.S. and Iran to end the war.
On Tuesday, the national average prices for gasoline sank below $4 a gallon for the first time in nearly four months, according to AAA.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile energy and food prices, rose 0.3% in October, in line with September but slightly above economists' forecasts.
Josh Hirt, senior U.S. economist for Vanguard, said in an email that elevated energy prices have led to a "longer-lasting shock pass-through" to core inflation, prompting the investment company to raise its year-end 2026 core inflation forecast to 3.2%.
What this means for interest rates
Wall Street analysts predicted that firmer inflation last month will spur the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates when it meets in December.
"This is the last look at CPI inflation the Fed will get before its December meeting, and it most likely seals the deal on a rate hike to close the year," James McCann, senior economist for investment strategy at Edward Jones, said in an email. The bigger question, he added, is whether the central bank will raise its benchmark rate by a quarter or half of a percentage point.
After the latest inflation data, CME Group's FedWatch tool showed an 85% chance the Fed would raise rates by 0.25 percentage points in December and a 15% chance of a 0.50 percentage-point hike.
The central bank stayed on the sidelines at its October meeting, although two Federal Open Market Committee members voted in favor of a rate hike.
During a conference in London on Tuesday, Christopher Waller, a member of the Fed's Board of Governors, said policymakers should consider a 0.50 percentage-point increase when the central bank meets on Dec. 8-9.
"Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take," he said.

sources.news_title: Inflation rose 0.4% last month, more than expected
sources.text:
The cost of everyday necessities continued to climb in October, putting more pressure on Americans already struggling to keep up with grocery bills, housing costs and other household expenses.
Consumer prices rose 0.4% from a month earlier, more than the 0.3% increase economists had anticipated, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics released Tuesday.
Nearly a third of the overall increase in prices came from shelter costs, which include rent and other housing-related expenses.
Stripping out food and energy prices, so-called “core” inflation rose 0.3%, matching the rate in September and August. The firmness in price increases beyond the pump suggests that inflation is continuing to broaden out.
No year-over-year inflation figure was available because last year’s government shutdown prevented the BLS from collecting most of the price data needed to make the comparison.
Economists, however, estimated the annual rate to be around 4%, which would mark an increase from September’s 3.7% annual inflation rate.
The report comes days after Democrats scored sweeping midterm victories, with frustration over the cost of living emerging as a major issue for voters.
Prices continue to rise faster than workers’ pay, meaning Americans’ earnings are losing ground to the cost of living.
Adding to the squeeze, the October inflation report all but guarantees the Federal Reserve will hike its benchmark interest rate at the December monetary policy meeting, making borrowing more expensive for households already struggling with higher costs.
Shortly before Tuesday’s data was released, Fed Governor Christopher Waller, a key voice on the central bank’s rate-setting committee, said that if core inflation came in at 0.3%, he would be inclined to support a half-point hike next month, twice the size of the Fed’s typical move
“I am particularly concerned about the breadth of price increases,” he said in remarks delivered at a Bank of England conference on Tuesday.
The Fed last raised rates in September by a quarter point, marking the first time in three years that it increased borrowing costs.
With the significant jump in mortgage rates over the past few years, more would-be homebuyers are being forced to rent. That’s putting upward pressure on the rental market, where prices increased 0.3% in October.
From baby formula to smartphones
At the onset of the war with Iran, price increases appeared to be predominantly stemming from skyrocketing energy costs. The big silver lining was that other key household expenses, such as food, appeared to be insulated.
That’s not quite true anymore: Last month, food prices rose 0.5%, accounting for nearly a fifth of the overall monthly price increase. That’s likely a reflection of the surge in diesel prices, which have significantly raised transportation costs.
Food, particularly produce, is especially vulnerable to price increases when input costs rise, given profit margins are typically thinner, making it harder for businesses to absorb price increases.
Baby food and formula surged 5.1% in October, the largest monthly increase since the BLS began tracking that category nearly 30 years ago.
Beef prices continued to climb in October, as strong demand and a limited cattle supply kept pressure on the market. Ground beef and steak each rose more than 1%.
Electronics continued to get more expensive, a likely byproduct of higher chip prices stemming from surging demand due to the AI buildout.
Smartphones increased 1.4% in October, the largest increase since the BLS began tracking them seven years ago. Television prices rose 3.3%.

sources.news_title: Consumer inflation rises faster than expected in October, CPI report shows
sources.text:
Consumer inflation rises faster than expected in October, CPI report shows
Labor Department releases closely watched October CPI inflation report
Inflation accelerated in October as the pace of consumer price growth trended higher.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said on Wednesday that the consumer price index (CPI) – a broad measure of how much everyday goods like gasoline, groceries and rent cost – increased 0.4% on a monthly basis.
It did not release an annual figure due to last year's government shutdown that prevented collection of October 2025 data.
FED'S PREFERRED INFLATION GAUGE ROSE IN SEPTEMBER AS THIRD-QUARTER GDP BEATS EXPECTATIONS
Expectations vs. reality
The monthly figure was slightly higher than the estimates of economists polled by LSEG, who expected inflation to rise 0.3% from the prior month.
So-called core prices, which exclude volatile measurements of gasoline and groceries to better assess price growth trends, were up 0.3% in October.
That figure is slightly higher than the 0.2% estimate of economists polled by LSEG. Like with headline CPI, the BLS was unable to release a year-over-year figure for core CPI due to last year's government shutdown disrupting data collection.
The cost of living breakdown
High inflation has created severe financial pressures in recent years for most U.S. households, which are forced to pay more for everyday necessities like food and rent. Price hikes are particularly difficult for lower-income Americans because they tend to spend more of their already-stretched paychecks on necessities and have less flexibility to save.
Energy prices rose 0.7% on a monthly basis in October, which is much cooler than the 5.2% reading in September and the 2.1% rise recorded in August. The energy index had experienced monthly drops earlier in the summer amid volatility in oil and gas prices due to the Iran war.
Gasoline prices increased 1% in October, which followed a similar cooling trend after readings of 9.1% in September and 3.9% in August.
Food prices were up 0.5% from the prior month in October, the largest increase for the broader index since April. The food at home index was up 0.4%, while the food away from home index rose 0.5% from the prior month.
FEDERAL RESERVE MAKES INTEREST RATE DECISION AHEAD OF MIDTERMS
The meats, poultry and fish index rose 0.5% last month. Beef and veal rose 0.9% in October, while egg prices increased 0.6%. The fruits and vegetables index increased 0.6% in October. Coffee prices fell 3.6% during the month.
Housing prices increased 0.3% on a monthly basis, while tenants' and household insurance costs were up 0.1% in October.
The transportation services index rose 0.8% in October with airfares rising 0.4% for the month.
What experts are saying
EY-Parthenon chief economist Gregory Daco said that "Inflation surprised to the upside in October, with broad-based pressures across food, goods and services."
"The hotter and broader inflation report likely seals the deal for a Fed rate hike in December. The latest employment report gives policymakers greater latitude to focus squarely on inflation for now. While the Fed justified its October hold by pointing to the lack of urgency to tighten policy, failing to deliver the expected December hike would risk calling into question its resolve to restore price stability," Daco added.
WHY THE FED ISN'T READY TO DECLARE VICTORY ON INFLATION
Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, said that the report showed that inflation remains the main problem facing the U.S. economy and that the "Federal Reserve has to act in December."
"Inflation came in hot in October and it wasn't just gas prices. Grocery prices jumped with the biggest monthly gain since April, and electricity saw another big gain," Long said. "This is painful for many Americans when so many basic necessities are rising in price."
Long added that while the BLS didn't publish the year-over-year CPI inflation figures due to the government shutdown last year, the "implied rate is around 4%, well above wage gains of 3.1% in the past year."
What does it mean for the Fed?
The Federal Reserve is set to hold its next monetary policy meeting on Dec. 8-9 and policymakers are overwhelmingly expected to hike interest rates in the wake of the October CPI inflation report.
The market sees an 87.3% probability of a 25-basis-point hike to a new target range of 4% to 4.25%, up from 84% a day ago and 77% a week ago, according to the CME FedWatch tool.
It also sees a 12.7% chance of a 50-basis-point rate hike in December, up from 0% yesterday and last week, while the tool showed the odds of the Fed leaving rates at their current level fell from 16% yesterday to 0%.

How did the market respond?
The benchmark S&P 500 Index fell more than 0.4% in Tuesday morning trading following the release of the October CPI inflation report.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average and Nasdaq Composite were also down a little more than 0.4%.

sources.news_title: Inflation ran hotter than expected last month, underscoring affordabil
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. inflation was higher than expected last month as the rising prices that powered sweeping Democratic victories in last week’s midterm elections appear likely to pose ongoing challenges for the White House and the Federal Reserve .
The consumer price index rose 0.4% from September to October, the Labor Department said Tuesday , down from 0.6% the previous month. The government did not report a yearly inflation rate because last year’s government shutdown meant no data was released for October 2025.
But excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 0.3%, the same as the preceding month. Both figures were a tenth of a point higher than forecast, and at an annual rate would be well above the Fed’s 2% target.
The new inflation data heightened concerns that strong consumer and business spending, combined with higher gas prices and supply disruptions stemming from tariffs and global turmoil , are creating increasingly stubborn inflation that could extend beyond temporary spikes in prices at the gas pump. The economy expanded at a 3.4% annual rate in the July-September quarter, mostly driven by consumer spending.
“It’s worrisome. There is a sense that inflation is broad, persistent, a little bit everywhere,” said Riccardo Trezzi, founder of Underlying Inflation, a consulting firm, and a former Fed economist. “The Fed should be very worried.”
Using rough estimates for last October’s data, Trezzi calculates that consumer prices rose 4% in October from a year ago, up from 3.7% in September. Core prices rose 2.8%, he estimates, up from 2.6%.
Americans’ struggles with high prices were evident as they ousted Republican majorities from the House and Senate last week . With historic gains in both chambers, Democrats in Congress will soon face the same challenges . President Donald Trump has acknowledged voter anger over the Iran war and gas prices but has shown no sign yet of changing course.
The AP Voter Poll , a survey of 100,000 voters, found about two-thirds blamed Trump’s policies for higher costs. About 9 in 10 said the cost of living was a “crucial” or “major” factor in their vote.
The persistence of elevated inflation makes it highly likely that the Fed will raise its key interest rate at its next meeting in December. It kept rates unchanged late last month , after raising them in September. The Fed increases borrowing costs in an effort to cool spending and bring down inflation.
Earlier Tuesday, Fed governor Christopher Waller, an outspoken member of the central bank’s rate-setting committee, said that a hike of a half-point next month was possible, double the size of the usual quarter-point increase.
“Economic activity is strong, the labor market is stable, but inflation is too high, well above” the Fed’s 2% goal, Waller said.
Stock prices fell in early trading Tuesday, and Treasury yields rose, on expectations of more persistent inflation and higher rates from the Fed.
Gas prices rose 1% from September to October, the government said, a stiff increase but still much lower than in previous months. Gas prices have soared more than 37% from a year ago. Still, oil prices have fallen sharply in recent days on hopes that the Iran conflict is fading, and gas costs have declined this month.
Yet there are signs higher energy prices are spreading into other parts of the economy, with air fares, public transportation, and delivery services all jumping in price. Electricity prices rose 0.9% from September to October, the most since April, and grocery prices jumped 0.4%, a painful rise after years of increases.
Beef prices rose 0.9% last month, after jumping nearly 14% in the first half of this year. Restaurant prices rose 0.5% from September to October, the most since January 2024. Rising shipping prices, driven up by more expensive gas, have lifted costs for restaurants and grocery stores, which may be passing them on to consumers.
Inflation has also been worsened by the massive investments flowing into artificial intelligence, which has contributed to higher prices for computer chips, electricity and consumer electronics. Voters swept dozens of candidates into office who had pledged to slow data center construction .
Computer prices jumped 0.5% last month, the government report showed, after rising nearly 10% in the year ending in September, lifted by more expensive chips. The cost of computers had been retreating for years as semiconductor chips became more efficient. That trend reversed course this year as prices rose sharply.
Prices are also rising in some sectors that have little to do with oil and gas or AI. Streaming video services have recently gotten more expensive, with Disney raising prices last month for its ad-supported Disney+ and Hulu streaming bundle to $12.49 a month from $11.99. The ad-free version rose by $2.50 to $21.49.
Prices also increased last month for an Apple TV/Peacock streaming bundle, to $17.99 from $14.99 a month.
Small businesses are bracing for a spending pullback by customers.
Chris Butler, CEO of National Tree Company, an artificial tree importer and wholesaler, says most of his customers now spend $200 or less on a tree. That is a big departure from the pandemic days when many people, flush with cash, were spending $300 to $400, he said.
“Inflation continues to persist,” he said. “Gas prices continue to be high, so consumers are hurting from a discretionary perspective.”
Last year, National Tree was forced to raise prices on its products, sourced in China and Cambodia, between 10% and 15% because of Trump’s tariffs, Butler said. Tariffs have come down, but now the firm is grappling with higher diesel costs.
Butler said the company, based in Cranford, N.J., doesn’t plan to raise prices again this year given the existing financial stress on customers, who are already spending less on trees.
Outside of inflation, other measures show the economy is largely doing well. The unemployment rate is a low 4.1% and growth is steady. Still, high prices have left most Americans with a dour view of the economy.
“It might not be a recession, but if you’re still living paycheck to paycheck and watching gas prices go up, grocery prices go up, your rent costs go up, it’s not going to feel like a robust economy,” said Jim Baird, chief investment officer at Plante Moran Financial Advisors.
___
AP Retail Writer Anne D’Innocenzio in New York contributed to this story.

sources.news_title: Monthly Inflation Slipped to 0.4% in October, but Remains Higher Than Expected
Prices post slowest rise in three months as gas costs drop
sources.text:
Prices rose 0.4% in October after the rising cost of gas eased throughout the month, bringing slight relief to consumers who have been hammered by high prices for most of the year.
In September, prices had jumped by 0.6% from August, meaning the pace of inflation cooled last month, but it nonetheless remains too elevated for comfort.
Core inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, rose 0.3% from September for the third straight month. Both readings from the Bureau of Labor Statistics were higher than economists had widely expected, underscoring the affordability pressures Americans faced as they voted out incumbent Republicans in last week’s midterm elections.
A higher-than-expected core inflation reading indicates soaring energy prices could be spilling over into the broader economy.
Price growth also continues to outpace wage increases, adding to strain on consumers. Diane Swonk, chief economist at KPMG, described the situation as “the worst bout of inflation relative to wage gains since the 1970s.”
Tuesday’s report includes no year-ago figures because of the government shutdown in October 2025, which forced the BLS to cancel that month’s inflation report.
Diesel prices spill over
The pace of inflation slowed slightly was largely the result of easing gas prices last month, which, according to motor club AAA’s average, fell from $4.41 per gallon Oct. 1 to $4.18 by the end of the month, a more than 5% drop.
But the BLS’ report showed that the overall gas price index still rose a solid 1%, even as the average nationwide price for a gallon of unleaded fell. Home heating oil also rose 2% from September, and electricity prices rose 0.9%.
Top White House officials acknowledged that inflation was troubling and had been worse than expected.
“It’s not a good number,” said Chris Phelan, chairman of the White House Council of Economic Advisers.
“I think that’s what we’re seeing is higher gas and diesel prices, due to high oil prices, filtering through the economy,” Phelan told Bloomberg TV.
He also described the inflation situation as a “cloud” over the economy. “I don’t want to say that this is a good number; it’s not.”
Kevin Hassett, director of the National Economic Council, called it “a disappointing report.”
“Right now, the trickle-down from the higher energy prices is definitely very palpable in the data,” he told Fox Business Network.
Earlier Tuesday, AAA data showed that average nationwide gas prices had fallen below $4 per gallon for the first time since July. In early trading, oil prices continued their recent sharp descent. Brent crude oil briefly tumbled below $90 after having been as high as $118 on Oct. 30.
But diesel fuel prices are 70% higher than at the start of the year, a far larger increase than regular gas experienced. Diesel is a major input cost for the transportation industry that delivers goods, such as groceries, to store shelves around the world.
Baby formula and groceries hit hard
Several other major consumer categories also put up strong rises over the month. Hospital services, vehicle insurance, dairy, and fruits and vegetables all showed large month-over-month price increases.
The price of baby food and infant formula posted its largest increase ever in October, rising 5.1%.
The price of smartphones also rose a record 1.4%, with prices most likely pushed higher by the AI boom. A demand for memory for data centers has caused dozens of consumer electronics companies, such as Apple, to hike prices.

Meanwhile, the “food at home” category, which follows grocery prices, rose the most since April.

Physicians’ services also jumped a similar amount, as did airfares. The price of new vehicles rose in October, although used car and truck prices fell by a sharp 1.2%.
Just weeks before the holiday season kicks off in earnest, the BLS reported that toy prices rose 1.8% in October.
The interest rate debate
There is a lot riding on this month’s inflation data. Economists had expected overall inflation to rise 0.3% and core inflation to rise 0.2%.
But even before Tuesday’s report, Federal Reserve governor Christopher Waller was significantly raising the stakes for what October’s inflation would mean.
“While I am hoping for an improvement over September, even if this occurs, I would still support a 25 basis-point increase” at the Fed’s Dec. 8-9 interest rate meeting, Waller said in a speech at a central banking conference in London earlier Tuesday.
“Let’s just say it. September’s inflation data were bad. There was no silver lining,” he continued. In September, inflation was on the upswing again and hit 3.7% on a year-over-year basis.
He surprised investors by going a step further, however.
“If inflation comes in substantially higher than I expect, more robust action by the [Fed] may be called for,” he said.
Specifically, if core inflation were to rise by 0.3% or higher, “I believe a 50 basis-point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting.”
The Fed has not hiked interest rates by a half-percent in one sitting since 2022.
The central bank traditionally favors multiple hikes of 0.25% in succession, so members can watch how each rate increase plays out.
“Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take,” Waller concluded.
Shortly after Waller spoke, the BLS announced that core inflation had, indeed, risen by 0.3% last month.
Hours later, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan supported Waller’s idea, saying the Fed “needs to implement at least two more 25 basis-point rate increases.” She added, “It may be possible to move more rapidly.”
Stocks fell in response to the data, led by the interest-rate- sensitive tech sector, followed closely by materials and industrial stocks. Those sectors are highly exposed to rate increases, as they raise hundreds of billions of dollars to build and fill up sprawling data centers.
U.S. Treasury yields moved sharply higher on the data, which could make mortgage loans more expensive if it holds up. And a Fed rate hike, of any magnitude, could make matters worse.
The 10-year Treasury yield again neared 5% Tuesday for the first time since the end of October.
Stocks fell in early trading Tuesday before they steadied midmorning to trade flat across the major indexes.

The cleanest numbers in the report are the paces: over the last six months prices rose at a 3.1% annual rate, and over the last three months at 5.7%, a stretch that includes September’s 9.1% jump in gasoline. Inside the report, grocery prices (food at home) rose 0.4%; energy overall rose 0.7%; gasoline rose 1.0% after a 9.1% jump in September; shelter rose 0.3%; electricity rose 0.9%; medical care rose 0.3%.
A hotter reading than forecasters expected is a warning that prices are still climbing faster than the Fed wants even with gasoline falling, and it makes a quarter-point rate increase on December 9 close to certain. It is also one month of data, and the Fed has never moved on a single print.
You already know the other number for next year. Social Security checks rise 3.6% in January, a raise set in October from the third-quarter CPI-W, so nothing in Tuesday’s report changes it. The question is what the report does to the rest of your money: the IRA that pays for everything Social Security does not, the cash earning 4%, and the Fed meeting on December 8 and 9. Here is the arithmetic for one couple.
Dennis and Joan
Dennis is 68, a retired electrical engineer. Joan is 66, a retired nurse. They have $2.2 million: $1,700,000 in a rollover IRA, $300,000 in a brokerage account and $200,000 in Treasury bills and a money market fund, $2,200,000 in all. Social Security pays him $3,000 a month and her $1,500, $54,000 a year. They spend $10,500 a month, $126,000 a year, so $72,000 comes out of the portfolio, 3.3% of it. Those are assumptions; put your own numbers beside them.
What the raise covers
In January their checks rise to $4,662 a month, $162 more, $1,944 a year. Medicare takes some of it back. The Part B premium is $202.90 a month this year, and the 2026 Medicare Trustees Report projects $209.50 for 2027, $6.60 more for each of them, so the net raise is about $148.80 a month if Medicare confirms that figure in the coming weeks. Your raise is 3.6% of your own check, so scale the numbers to it.
Now the costs. At the six-month pace of 3.1%, their $126,000 of spending rises by $3,906 next year, and the raise covers 50% of that. At the three-month pace of 5.7% the bill rises by $7,182 and the raise covers 27%. Social Security pays 43% of their bills, and it is the only part of their income with a cost-of-living clause. The other 57% comes from savings, and savings get no raise.
| Line | 2026 | 2027 at the 3.1% pace | 2027 at the 5.7% pace | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Spending | $126,000 | $129,906 | $133,182 | 
| Social Security | $54,000 | $55,944 | $55,944 | 
| Portfolio draw | $72,000 | $73,962 | $77,238 | 
| Draw as a share of $2,200,000 | 3.3% | 3.4% | 3.5% | 
What the IRA has to cover
The draw rises from $72,000 to $73,962 at the six-month pace, $1,962 more. The IRA pays that, and the IRS taxes every dollar of it. Dennis and Joan are in the 12% bracket: 85% of their Social Security is already taxable, their standard deduction with the over-65 additions is $35,500, and the $6,000 senior deduction each brings their deductions to $47,500 against about $121,900 of income, leaving taxable income of about $74,400, with $26,400 of room before the 22% bracket. So every extra $1,000 of spending takes a $1,136 withdrawal, and the extra draw costs $2,230 out of the IRA at the six-month pace, $5,952 at the three-month pace. If you are in the 22% bracket, each $1,000 of spending takes $1,282 from your IRA.
The number that does not show on any statement is the standstill cost: at the six-month pace, $2,200,000 that earns nothing loses $68,200 of buying power in a year. Every dollar you hold has to earn 3.1% just to stay where it is, and a bank account paying 1% loses ground at any of these paces.
The cash and the Fed
Their $200,000 in bills earns about 4.17%, the three-month Treasury rate on November 5, $8,340 a year, which is 1.1 points above the six-month pace of prices. The 10-year Treasury yields 4.84%, 1.7 points above it. Those real yields exist because the Fed raised rates in September and is expected to do it again: before the report, CME’s FedWatch tool put the odds of a quarter-point increase on December 9 at 84%. Nothing in Tuesday’s numbers argues against it. Bank of America’s Stephen Juneau wrote before the report that a print at his forecast "would effectively lock in another 25bp hike, all else equal." A quarter point adds about $500 a year to the couple’s bill income.
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh told reporters on October 28 that "interest rates get in the cracks" and "affect directly or indirectly, almost everything." For you that cuts both ways. The bill ladder resets every three months, so if the Fed stops after December, so does the 4%. A two-year Treasury at 4.51% or a five-year ladder holds the yield longer, at the price of a smaller gain if rates keep rising.
Stocks had their best day since April on Monday, with the S&P 500 fund up 2.36%, as oil fell: Brent settled at $92.57, $43 below its October 2 high of $135.51, and the national average for regular gasoline was $4.15 a gallon in the week of November 2, down from $4.27 a week earlier, according to the Energy Information Administration. That is where October’s energy relief came from. The report does not say what stocks do next, and neither does this.
Where this goes wrong
Three places. The six-month pace smooths one jump and one drop in gasoline, and if your own bills run closer to the three-month pace, use that column; if oil stays near $92 the headline rate cools further, and if the talks to end the Iran war fail it does not. The Part B figure is a projection until the government publishes the real one. And the 3.6% raise is fixed for all of 2027 whatever prices do: if inflation runs at the three-month pace of 5.7%, the raise falls behind by 2.1 points; at the six-month pace of 3.1%, it stays ahead by 0.5 points.
The bottom line
October’s inflation report changed nothing about your Social Security raise and made the December rate increase harder to doubt. For Dennis and Joan the raise covers 50% of next year’s higher costs at the six-month pace and 27% at the three-month pace, and the IRA covers the rest, $2,230 to $5,952 more before tax. Keep a year of the draw in bills while they pay 4%, size the withdrawal to the pace you see in your own bills, and do not sell stocks on one inflation number: the raise is fixed, the pace is not.

sources.news_title: Consumer Prices Rise More Than Expected as Shelter and Food Prices Jump
sources.text:
The consumer price index rose 0.4 percent in October compared with September, the Labor Department said Tuesday.
Core prices, a measure that excludes food and energy prices, rose 0.3 percent.
Economists had forecast overall inflation at 0.3 percent. Core prices were expected to rise 0.2 percent.
The September increase was estimated at 0.6 percent for overall inflation and 0.3 percent for core inflation.
There was no estimate for year-over-year prices released due to the government shutdown last October. This prevented the government from collecting and releasing the CPI 12 months ago.
The three-month annualized rate of headline inflation comes to 5.7 percent and three-month core CPI is up 3.7 percent. Six-month annualized CPI is up 3.1 percent and core is up 2.7 percent. This indicates a sustained and significant acceleration of inflation.
Shelter prices rose 0.3 percent in October, which the Department of Labor said accounted for over thirty percent of the monthly all items increase. Food prices rose 0.5 percent in October, as the food at home index—which covers grocery prices—rose 0.4 percent and the food away from home index—basically, restaurant prices—increased 0.5 percent.
The index for energy increased 0.7 percent over the month following a 5.2-percent increase in September, including a one percent increase in the price of gasoline.
The higher-than-expected rate of inflation boosted bets in the derivatives market that the Federal Reserve will increase interest rates when it meets next month. Investors increasingly expect the Fed may raise interest rates by a half percentage point, a bigger increase than the quarter-point increase expected earlier.
The report indicates inflationary pressures are spreading out from oil prices and closely related goods and services. Household furnishing prices rose 0.7 percent. Major appliance prices jumped 1.4 percent. Medical drug prices, which have been falling in recent months, rose by 0.4 percent. High-tech goods rose 0.4 percent.
Prices of many services rose sharply. The overall category of services excluding energy services rose 0.3 percent. Recreation prices jumped 0.8 percent, as did hospital services. Hotel and motel prices rose 0.7 percent. Motor vehicle insurance prices rose 0.7 percent. Physician services rose 0.4 percent. Airline fares rose 0.4 percent.
So-called super core services inflation—which excludes energy and housing prices—rose by 0.5 percent.

sources.news_title: Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, more than expected, complicating Fed's inflation fight
sources.text:
Costs for goods and services rose more than expected in October, providing fresh warning signs for the Federal Reserve in its fight to lower inflation.
The consumer price index, a broad gauge of costs across the U.S. economy, increased a seasonally adjusted 0.4% for the month, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Tuesday. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones had been looking for a 0.3% increase.
Stripping out volatile food and energy, so-called core CPI increased 0.3% against the forecast for a 0.2% gain.
The headline CPI had increased 0.6% in September while core was up 0.3%.
The report comes at a critical juncture for the Federal Reserve as it considers its next interest-rate move. Speaking Tuesday morning in London ahead of the CPI release, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a hot inflation report could push him toward advocating for a half-point increase in December, and specifically said such a hike should be on the table if core CPI was "around 0.3."
Hours later, that's exactly what happened.
Traders are now fully pricing in a quarter percentage-point increase when the Fed next meets Dec. 8-9, and put odds of a half-point hike at 13.6%, after being around zero prior to the inflation report, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.
Stocks fell following the release, while Treasury yields jumped.
"This was the report the market could least afford to see," said Karen Manna, fixed income investment strategist at Federated Hermes. "A hotter inflation print raises fresh questions about whether the Fed has done enough to contain price pressures and reinforces the risk that interest rates need to move higher and stay there for longer."
The BLS did not estimate a yearly rate in its October inflation report. The government shutdown last year prevented the bureau from collecting sufficient data in October 2025, so there is no comparable figure to use. However, the report did include annual figures for some individual items where it was able to collect data.
Though gasoline prices have been falling in recent weeks, the energy index rose 0.7% and the gasoline index was up 1%. The natural gas index, though, was off 0.8%.
Food costs accelerated 0.5%, pushed higher by increases of 1% for snacks, 0.9% for beef and 0.5% for meats, poultry, fish and eggs. Transportation services jumped 0.8%. New vehicle prices increased 0.2% but used cars and trucks fell 1.2%.
Shelter costs were higher by 0.3%, which the BLS said accounted for more than 30% of the headline increase.
Apparel, a tariff-sensitive sector, rose just 0.1%. Medical care commodities prices increased 0.5%. Airline fares accelerated 0.4%.
At the Fed's October meeting, central bank officials voted 10-2 to keep their benchmark rate in a range between 3.75%-4% while awaiting incoming data.
Markets already had been expecting the Fed to hike its benchmark borrowing rate next month, but the inflation data may have sealed the deal.
Despite the moderating gas prices recently, Fed officials have expressed concern that the impacts from the Iran war and President Donald Trump's tariffs are becoming embedded in the economy. Inflation has been running above the Fed's 2% target for some 5½ years.
Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, speaking Tuesday after the inflation report, said she sees a need for two additional quarter-point increases. Logan noted that the CPI report was "higher than expected" and said she is worried that the Fed's primary inflation-forecasting metric, the personal consumption expenditures price index, also could move higher when it is reported later in November.
"It may be possible to move more rapidly this winter than the [Federal Open Market Committee] has moved so far this fall," she said. "After two more increases are in place, it would make sense in my view to pause and examine economic and financial developments to determine what further action may be appropriate."
In addition to tariffs and the war, inflation has been pressured by hyperscaler spending in the artificial intelligence buildout. Electricity prices rose 0.9%, a potential complication from the AI story.
Anna Paulson, the president of the Philadelphia Fed, listed tariffs, energy prices, and the AI buildout as the "main factors have been keeping inflation elevated," in remarks later Tuesday, though she pointed to research that said the effects from tariffs were "beginning to fade."
But she said the Tuesday data suggest "inflation pressures are still very much with us."
"For now, further gradual tightening seems appropriate," said Paulson in her prepared remarks. "But the exact path will depend on how conditions evolve, and I'll be watching the data closely."
For now, consumers continue to spend — retail sales rose 0.8% in September, according to the Commerce Department — but businesses plan more price hikes.
A net 37% of businesses responding to the October National Federation of Independent Business survey reported that they plan to raise prices in the next three months, the highest level since July 2022.

sources.text:
U.S. consumer prices increased more than expected in October, driven by higher costs for food and accommodation, leaving the Federal Reserve on course to raise interest rates next month.
The Consumer Price Index report from the Labor Department on Tuesday also showed a strong buildup of underlying inflation pressures for the third straight month. The Labor Department’s Bureau of Labor Statistics did not publish year-over-year inflation readings because last year’s federal government shutdown prevented the collection of consumer price data in October 2025, leaving no comparison base.
Annual consumer inflation jumped 3.7 per cent in September. Inflation is running well above the U.S. central bank’s 2-per-cent target.
The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has boosted oil prices, combining with the import tariffs implemented by the Trump administration last year to lift the cost of living. High inflation contributed to the heavy losses suffered by President Donald Trump’s Republican Party in the midterm elections last week.
Fed Governor Christopher Waller said on Tuesday that the U.S. central bank should raise rates next month, adding that “a stronger policy move may be needed.” Waller also raised the prospect of a 50-basis-point hike if core consumer prices, excluding food and energy, increased 0.3 per cent or more from September, which they did.
“Consumers’ inflation nightmare continues with no relief in sight,” said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. “Fed officials are going to need to bring a bigger hose if they have any hope of putting the inflation fire out.”
The CPI increased 0.4 per cent last month after advancing 0.6 per cent in September. It was the third consecutive month of CPI gains of 0.4 per cent or more. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the CPI climbing 0.3 per cent over the month.
Shelter, which includes rents, hotel and motel rooms, accounted for more than 30 per cent of the increase in the CPI last month. Shelter costs rose 0.3 per cent after climbing 0.4 per cent in September.
Food prices surged 0.5 per cent after barely rising in the prior three months. Grocery store prices rebounded 0.4 per cent, boosted by a 0.9 per cent jump in the cost of beef. Egg prices rose 0.6 per cent while fruits and vegetables were 0.6 per cent more expensive. Prices for dairy and related products rose 0.6 per cent. The cost of snacks surged 1.0 per cent.
Higher prices at the supermarket could be a reflection of more expensive diesel fuel. The cost of eating out also increased last month, with prices of food away from home surging 0.5 per cent after rising 0.2 per cent in September. The cost of full service meals increased 0.7 per cent.
Gasoline prices climbed 1.0 per cent after soaring 9.1 per cent. Though diesel prices have come down from record highs, they rose 2.7 per cent last month after increasing 11.9 per cent in September.
Strong core inflation
Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the CPI increased 0.3 per cent in October, advancing by the same margin for three months in a row. The so-called core CPI was forecast to have climbed 0.2 per cent in October. Core CPI inflation increased 2.6 per cent year-over-year in September. It was last month driven by a 0.3 per cent rise in owners’ equivalent rent, a measure of the amount homeowners would pay to rent or would earn from renting their property.
Prices for hotel and motel rooms rose 0.6 per cent. Airline fares rose 0.4 per cent. The cost of recreation increased 0.8 per cent, while motor vehicle insurance advanced 0.7 per cent. Household furnishings and supplies prices rebounded 0.7 per cent, suggesting that some pass-through from tariffs remained. There were also increases in the prices of new vehicles, medication and recreation goods.
Financial markets were pricing in a roughly 89 per cent chance of a 25-basis-points rate hike next month. The Fed left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75-4.00 per cent range last month. Economists said only a substantial sell-off on the equity markets or widening credit spreads would prevent the Fed from tightening monetary policy in December.
US stocks opened lower. They slumped last week after the Democrats’ sweeping victory fanned fears that new regulations could dent the durability of the AI trade, but rallied on Monday as oil prices fell. The dollar gained versus a basket of currencies. US Treasury yields rose.
The missing data from last year have no impact on the calculation of the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index readings that are tracked by the Fed to gauge progress toward its inflation target. Both measures are running above 3 per cent.

U.S. markets dipped immediately after the inflation report and Treasury yields ticked higher, on expectations of more persistent inflation and higher rates from the Fed.

Inflation has also been worsened by rampant investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure, which has contributed to higher prices for computer chips, electricity and consumer electronics. Voters swept dozens of candidates into office who had pledged to slow data center construction.
Prices are also rising in some sectors that have little to do with oil and gas or AI. Streaming video services have recently gotten more expensive, with Disney raising prices last month for its ad-supported Disney+ and Hulu streaming bundle to $12.49 a month from $11.99. sources.news_title: US stocks fall after worse-than-expected report on inflation
sources.text: NEW YORK (AP) — The U.S. stock market dipped Tuesday after a report showed inflation was worse across the country last month than economists expected. The S&P 500 slipped 0.4% and gave back some of its big rally from the day before. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 157 points, or 0.3%, and the Nasdaq composite sank 0.7%. Pressure from the bond market undercut stocks following the discouraging report on inflation. People had to pay prices for groceries, electricity and other costs of living that were higher last month than economists expected. That could push the Federal Reserve to hike its main interest rate at its next meeting in December and beyond. Higher interest rates can help rein in inflation, but they do so by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money and by slowing the overall economy. Higher rates also make investors less willing to pay high prices for stocks and other investments. Speaking in London before the inflation report was released, Fed Gov. Micron Technology, which sells memory for computers, fell 1.1%. CoreWeave, a company that rents out access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, slipped 0.5%. Other AI-related stocks held up better, though. Broadcom climbed 3.9%, and Advanced Micro Devices rose 1.3%. sources.text:
Inflation slowed in October but exceeded expectations as higher food and shelter costs continued to pressure U.S. consumers, according to figures released Tuesday by the Labor Department. The report also lacked an annual inflation rate because of missing data from last year’s government shutdown.
Prices paid by U.S. consumers rose 0.4% in October, according to the latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) report from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, slowing from a 0.6% increase in September but exceeding forecasts for a 0.3% gain.
The CPI, a key measure of inflation, tracks changes in prices paid by American consumers for a broad range of goods and services, from groceries to gasoline.
Unlike most monthly releases, the October report did not include an overall annual inflation rate. The 2025 government shutdown prevented the BLS from collecting October 2025 price data, leaving it unable to calculate year-over-year changes for most categories. September’s headline inflation rate of 3.7% and core rate of 2.6% remain the latest available annual figures.
Looking at food costs, prices increased 0.5% in October after holding steady in September. Grocery prices climbed 0.4% following a 0.1% decline, while restaurant prices rose 0.5% after a 0.2% gain the previous month.
Among grocery categories, beef prices rose 0.9%, while fruits and vegetables and dairy products each increased 0.6%. Snack prices advanced 1.0%. In contrast, nonalcoholic beverage prices fell 0.3%, and cereals and bakery products were unchanged.
Energy prices continued to rise in October, but at a substantially slower pace than in September. Gasoline prices increased 1.0% after surging 9.1% the previous month. Despite the slowdown, pump prices were 37.4% higher than a year earlier, one of the few annual comparisons available in the report.
The broader energy index, which includes gasoline, electricity and fuel oil, advanced 0.7% in October following a 5.2% jump in September. Electricity prices climbed 0.9%, while natural gas prices declined 0.8%. Fuel oil prices rose 2.0%.
Excluding the volatile food and energy components, core consumer prices rose 0.3% in October for the third consecutive month, exceeding forecasts for a 0.2% increase.
Shelter costs climbed 0.3% in October after rising 0.4% in September, accounting for more than 30% of the overall monthly CPI increase. Owners’ equivalent rent increased 0.3%, while residential rents rose 0.2%. Lodging away from home, including hotels and motels, advanced 0.6% following a 2.0% increase in September.
The shelter component of the CPI includes apartment rents, owners’ equivalent rent — an estimate of what homeowners would pay to rent their homes — lodging away from home, housing at schools, and tenants’ and household insurance.
In other key categories:
- Clothing prices edged up 0.1% in October after rising 0.3% in September.
- New vehicle prices increased 0.2% for the second consecutive month and were 0.7% higher than a year earlier.
- Used car and truck prices fell 1.2% in October after climbing 0.7% in September and were 3.3% lower than a year ago.
- Airline fares rose 0.4% in October, slowing from increases of 1.2% in September and 2.7% in August.
- Recreation prices climbed 0.8% after rising 0.5% in September, while motor vehicle insurance increased 0.7%.
- Medical care costs advanced 0.3%, with hospital services rising 0.8% and physicians’ services increasing 0.4%.
The latest available headline annual inflation rate was 3.7% in September, up from 3.4% in August.
Similarly, annual core inflation last stood at 2.6% in September, compared with 2.4% in August. The core CPI, also known as the "all items less food and energy" index, is among the inflation measures monitored by Federal Reserve policymakers to assess price trends and guide monetary policy decisions.

The Fed doesn’t set mortgage rates, but when the market expects more hikes, bond investors demand higher yields, and mortgage rates follow bond yields up.
Whether the Fed hikes that much or not, it’s a major setback for mortgage rates, which had enjoyed a really good spell over the past month.
In fact, they were inching closer and closer to a 6-handle again before we got a hot jobs report Friday and hot CPI today.
Was the Recent Drop in Mortgage Rates Just a Head Fake?
The average 30-year fixed fell from a rate of around 7.625% in early October to nearly 7.125% last week thanks to a combination of a tech selloff and cheaper oil prices.
Things were clearly trending lower and it almost appeared like the worst was behind us, yet again.
It really seemed like we could have moved even lower this week and beyond, but today’s CPI report had other ideas.
I always say nothing moves in a straight line, especially mortgage rates, so maybe it’s just the expected ebb and flow.
The worry though is this latest CPI report could be the start of another uptrend in rates, especially if odds rise for a 50-bp hike next month.
You start to wonder where the relief will come from if tech already sold off and the war is relatively clam.
As always, keep an eye on the economic data as it’s released, and another eye on the Middle East conflict.
Lastly, watch the stock market to see if the tech rout ratchets up again or cools off for the year.
If we get another flight to safety, that could help mortgage rates move lower, though it might be less impactful thanks to this latest inflation report.

The cost of goods and services rose more than expected in October, sending fresh warning signs for the Federal Reserve, CNBC reported.
The CPI, a broad gauge of costs across the U.S. economy, increased a seasonally adjusted 0.4% for the month, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Tuesday. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones had expected a 0.3% increase, CNBC noted.
Stripping out volatile food and energy, so-called core CPI increased 0.3% against the forecast for a 0.2% gain, the BLS reported.
The headline CPI had increased 0.6% in September while core was up 0.3%.
CNBC noted that the report comes at a critical point for the Federal Reserve as it considers its next interest-rate move.
Hot Inflation Report
Speaking Tuesday in London ahead of the CPI release, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a hot inflation report could push him toward advocating for a half-point increase in December, and specifically said such a hike should be on the table if core CPI was “around 0.3.”
And that’s what happened.
The Consumer Price Index is one of the most important economic indicators influencing mortgage rates because it measures inflation. When inflation rises, mortgage rates generally face upward pressure. When inflation falls, mortgage rates often have room to decline. That relationship is not automatic, however.
Mortgage rates respond primarily to inflation expectations, Treasury yields, and the bond market’s interpretation of CPI data.
Traders are now fully pricing in a quarter percentage-point increase when the Fed next meets Dec. 8-9, and they put odds of a half-point hike at 13.6%, after being around zero prior to the inflation report, according to the CME Group’s FedWatch tool.
Following the BLS release, stocks fell while Treasury yields jumped.
“This was the report the market could least afford to see,” said Karen Manna, fixed income investment strategist at Federated Hermes. “A hotter inflation print raises fresh questions about whether the Fed has done enough to contain price pressures and reinforces the risk that interest rates need to move higher and stay there for longer.”
The bureau did not estimate a yearly rate in its October inflation report.
No YoY Figures
The government shutdown last year prevented it from collecting sufficient data in October 2025, so there is no comparable figure to use. However, the report did include annual figures for some individual items where it was able to collect data.
Though gasoline prices have been falling in recent weeks, the energy index rose 0.7%, and the gasoline index was up 1%. The natural gas index, though, was off 0.8%.
Food costs accelerated 0.5%, pushed higher by increases of 1% for snacks, 0.9% for beef and 0.5% for meats, poultry, fish and eggs. Transportation services jumped 0.8%. New vehicle prices increased 0.2% but used cars and trucks fell 1.2%.
Shelter costs were higher by 0.3%, which the BLS said accounted for more than 30% of the headline increase.
Apparel, a tariff-sensitive sector, rose just 0.1%. Medical care commodities prices increased 0.5%. Airline fares accelerated 0.4%.
At its October meeting, central bank officials voted 10-2 to keep their benchmark rate in a range between 3.75%-4% while awaiting incoming data.
Markets already had been expecting the Fed to hike its benchmark borrowing rate next month, but the inflation data may have sealed the deal, CNBC said.
High Inflation for Years
Despite the moderating gas prices recently, Fed officials have expressed concern that the impacts from the Iran war and President Donald Trump’s tariffs are becoming embedded in the economy. Inflation has been running above the Fed’s 2% target for some 5½ years.
Speaking after the BLS report was released, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said she sees a need for two additional quarter-point increases. She noted that the CPI report was “higher than expected” and she is worried that the Fed’s primary inflation-forecasting metric, the personal consumption expenditures price index, also could move higher when it is reported later in November.
“It may be possible to move more rapidly this winter than the [Federal Open Market Committee] has moved so far this fall,” she said. “After two more increases are in place, it would make sense in my view to pause and examine economic and financial developments to determine what further action may be appropriate.”
In addition to tariffs and the war, inflation has been pressured by hyperscaler spending in the artificial intelligence buildout. Electricity prices rose 0.9%, a potential complication from the AI story.
Leaves Few Options
First American Senior Economist Sam Williamson noted that hot inflation leaves the Fed with few options but to hike rates in December.
“Inflation ran hotter than expected in October, with price pressures firming across the economy as earlier disinflationary tailwinds showed signs of fading. That keeps a December rate hike firmly on the table, putting a floor under mortgage rates and leaving life events, including new jobs, marriages and growing families, as the housing market’s main source of momentum,” Williamson noted.
“That puts the Federal Reserve under growing pressure to act after leaving rates unchanged last month. With the labor market showing remarkable resilience and inflation moving in the wrong direction, policymakers have fewer reasons to hold back. That keeps a December rate hike firmly on the table, a move that would further unwind the insurance cuts delivered late last year,” Williamson added.
“For home buyers, hotter inflation is likely to prolong the wait for meaningful mortgage-rate relief. Stronger job growth may give some households the income to move, but elevated borrowing costs raise the hurdle for everyone. Until mortgage rates ease, life moves will keep the housing market moving, while discretionary buyers wait on the sidelines,” he said.

Inflation Persists in October
sources.text:
Inflation remained elevated in October even as energy prices eased, raising expectations of another Fed rate hike. Shelter returned as the largest driver of headline inflation, accounting for over 30% of the monthly increase. Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy components, rose by 0.3% for the third consecutive month, suggesting broad-based price pressures across the economy. The Bureau of Labor Statistics did not release the annual inflation figure this month as October 2025 data is unavailable for comparison due to last year’s government shutdown.
On a monthly basis, the CPI rose by 0.4% in October (seasonally adjusted), while the “core” CPI increased by 0.3%. The monthly increase in core CPI has remained at 0.3% since August.
The price index for a broad set of energy sources increased by 0.7% in October, as decline in natural gas (-0.8%) was offset by increases in fuel oil (+2.0%), gasoline (+1.0%) and electricity (+0.9%). Meanwhile, the food at home and food away from home indexes rose by 0.4% and 0.5% respectively.
Outside of energy, other top contributors that rose in October included indexes for recreation (+%), medical care (+0.3%), motor vehicle insurance (+0.7%), household furnishings and operations (+0.2%) and education (+0.3%). Meanwhile, the indexes for used cars and trucks (-1.2%) and communication (-0.1%) were among the major indexes that decreased over the month.
The index for shelter, which makes up more than 40% of the “core” CPI, rose by 0.3% in October, following the same increase last month. The index for owners’ equivalent rent (OER) and rent of primary residence (RPR) increased by 0.3% and 0.2% over the month.
NAHB constructs a “real” rent index to indicate whether inflation in rents is faster or slower than core inflation. It provides insight into the supply and demand conditions for rental housing. When inflation in rents is rising faster than core inflation, the real rent index rises and vice versa. The real rent index is calculated by dividing the price index for rent by the core CPI (to exclude the volatile food and energy components). In October, the Real Rent Index fell by 0.1%.

Bitcoin Trades Near $73K as US CPI Increased to 0.4% in October from its expectations of 0.3%
Bitcoin trades near $73,000 after October US CPI exceeds expectations, strengthening December rate hike bets and adding pressure to an already struggling crypto market.
By Bikash DekaAuthor
Bitcoin trades near $73,000 after October US inflation came in hotter than economists expected, adding fresh pressure to an already struggling cryptocurrency market. Ethereum also weakened, while traders increased bets that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates at its December meeting.
The US Consumer Price Index (CPI) increased 0.4% month over month in October, beating expectations of 0.3%. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, climbed 0.3% against forecasts of 0.2%. The figures strengthened concerns that inflation is not cooling quickly enough, potentially keeping financial conditions tighter for longer.
Bitcoin Trades Near $73,000 After Inflation Surprise
Bitcoin was trading near $74,300 shortly before the October CPI release. It quickly slipped to approximately $73,400 after the report, briefly falling below the $74,000 level.
Ethereum also weakened, trading around $2,100 as investors reassessed the outlook for interest rates.
The inflation report showed that food prices increased 0.5% during October, while energy prices climbed 0.7%. Shelter costs, another important component of inflation, rose 0.3%.
These increases matter for cryptocurrency markets because persistent inflation can reduce expectations for monetary easing. When interest rates remain high or rise further, investors may become less willing to hold volatile assets such as Bitcoin and Ethereum.
The latest decline also follows a difficult period for Bitcoin ETFs. As we reported in our coverage of Bitcoin ETF outflows reaching $1.28 billion, institutional fund demand has weakened, adding another source of pressure to the market.
Fed Rate Hike Bets Increase After Hot CPI
The October inflation figures have strengthened expectations for a Federal Reserve rate increase in December.
According to Reuters, futures markets now price in virtually a 100% probability of a rate increase at the December 8–9 meeting. Most of that probability is concentrated on a 25-basis-point increase, although expectations for a larger 50-basis-point move have also increased to nearly 15%.
Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller's recent comments have added to the concerns. He indicated that a 50-basis-point increase should be considered if inflation came in hotter than expected.
The latest core CPI reading of 0.3% met the threshold Waller had highlighted.
For crypto investors, the concern is straightforward. Higher interest rates can make traditional financial instruments more attractive relative to assets that do not generate interest income. They can also strengthen the US dollar and reduce liquidity available for speculative investments.
Crypto Liquidations Add to Bitcoin's Selling Pressure
The CPI announcement arrived after an already significant liquidation event.
More than $1.15 billion in cryptocurrency positions were liquidated over a 24-hour period leading into November 10, including approximately $1.04 billion in long positions. Bitcoin and Ethereum traders accounted for a substantial portion of the losses.
Long positions are leveraged bets that prices will increase. When markets move sharply in the opposite direction, exchanges automatically close positions that no longer meet margin requirements.
These forced closures can intensify selling pressure, particularly when market sentiment is already weak.
The latest CPI release adds another challenge for traders who were hoping for a recovery. With Bitcoin struggling to remain above $74,000, market participants will be watching whether buyers step in around the recent lows or whether another wave of selling develops.
What Comes Next for Bitcoin and Ethereum?
The Federal Reserve's December meeting is now a major focus for cryptocurrency investors. Traders will continue monitoring upcoming inflation reports, employment figures and comments from policymakers for clues about the likely size of the next rate move.
The October CPI report does not guarantee that the Fed will raise rates by 50 basis points. However, it has made the possibility more relevant to market pricing.
For Bitcoin, holding above the recent $73,000 - $73,500 area could help limit further downside pressure. A sustained recovery would require stronger buying demand, particularly as ETF outflows and leveraged liquidations continue to influence market sentiment.
Ethereum and other altcoins could also remain vulnerable if investors continue moving away from riskier assets.
For now, the combination of sticky inflation, tighter monetary policy expectations and weak institutional demand is making a cryptocurrency market recovery more difficult.

sources.text:
U.S. consumer prices rose 0.4% in October from the previous month, a tenth of a point above economists’ forecasts, while core inflation, which strips out food and energy, came in at 0.3%, also above expectations. It’s becoming harder to imagine the Federal Reserve holding off much longer on another rate increase.
Markets reacted within hours: Treasury yields rose, stocks slipped, and according to CME Group’s tools, a quarter-point hike at the Fed’s Dec. 8-9 meeting is now considered nearly certain, with a non-trivial chance, around 14%, that the increase could be double that. Just last month, the central bank’s board chose caution, holding rates steady in a 10-2 vote and opting to wait for more data before moving again. That data has now arrived, and it points in the wrong direction.
Gas, meat and rent: where the pressure shows
Behind the headline number are specific drivers. Housing costs alone account for more than a third of the monthly increase. Energy still weighs heavily, even though pump prices had been falling in recent weeks, a sign that the decline hasn’t fully filtered through to the broader index yet: gasoline and fuel costs turned higher again. The grocery cart tells a simpler story, with meat and snacks leading an acceleration in food prices. Add to that a less obvious factor: the AI investment boom is pushing up electricity consumption among major tech companies, and with it household bills, a channel for inflation few would have predicted until recently.
An inflation problem that won’t quit after five years
For the Fed, the issue isn’t just October’s number. U.S. inflation has now stayed above the central bank’s 2% target for five and a half years, an unusually long stretch by its own standards, and officials are increasingly worried that the effects of the Iran war and President Donald Trump’s tariffs have become embedded in pricing behavior rather than remaining temporary shocks destined to fade on their own. Speaking in London hours before the data’s release, Fed Governor Christopher Waller had already suggested that a hotter-than-expected inflation reading could push him to back a more aggressive move in December, a half-point hike rather than a quarter-point one, stressing the importance of not disappointing market expectations.
“This was the report the market could least afford to see,” said Karen Manna of Federated Hermes, summing up the anxiety of those who feared exactly this scenario: rates forced higher still, and likely to stay elevated longer than expected.
Consumers, meanwhile, keep spending
What continues to surprise in this environment is the resilience of demand: retail sales had already risen 0.8% in September, and American businesses, far from pulling back, are planning further price increases. According to the latest National Federation of Independent Business survey, more than a third of small businesses polled plan to raise prices over the next three months, a level of pricing confidence not seen since the summer of 2022, at the start of the post-pandemic inflation surge.

Washington, November 10, 2026, 10:05 (EST)
U.S. consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, Tuesday’s government report showed. Monthly energy-price growth slowed by roughly 87%, but core inflation showed no improvement, leaving a weaker headline increase alongside persistent underlying price pressure.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics release showed energy inflation slowed to 0.7% from September’s 5.2%. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3% for a third consecutive month, leaving its pace unchanged despite the energy slowdown.
The unchanged core reading bears on the Federal Reserve’s December debate. Before the release, Governor Christopher Waller said similar readings could justify stronger action. In his prepared remarks in London, he set that threshold at monthly core CPI around 0.3% or higher.
TS2 calculates an 86.5% slowdown in energy’s monthly inflation rate. Subtracting 0.7 from 5.2 gives 4.5 percentage points; dividing by 5.2 gives the relative decline. The calculation compares rates of increase, not price levels or energy’s contribution to total inflation.
Slower energy, steady core
Monthly change, percent; seasonally adjusted. September → October 2026.
| Measure | Sep → Oct | 
|---|---|
| Headline CPI | 0.6% → 0.4% | 
| Core CPI | 0.3% → 0.3% | 
| Energy | 5.2% → 0.7% | 
| Gasoline | 9.1% → 1.0% | 
Source: BLS, Table A. As of November 10, 2026.
Energy prices continued to rise, as did the overall consumer basket, though its monthly increase slowed by 0.2 percentage points. The two measures have different basket weights, so an 87% slowdown in energy-price growth does not imply a comparable slowdown in headline inflation.
Gasoline shows the difference between adjusted and unadjusted prices. Its seasonally adjusted index rose 1.0%, following September’s 9.1% jump. Before seasonal adjustment, gasoline prices fell 0.7% in October. Both readings appear in the same BLS release but reflect different comparisons.
Household utility costs were mixed. Electricity inflation accelerated to 0.9% from 0.2% in September. Piped natural-gas prices fell 0.8% after a 0.3% decline. The broader energy-services index rose 0.6%, compared with 0.1% a month earlier.
Food provided less relief than the energy aggregate. Grocery prices rose 0.4%, reversing September’s 0.1% decline. Total food prices increased 0.5% after holding steady. These monthly index changes are not dollar estimates for any household’s purchases.
Four of the six major grocery food-group indexes rose. Fruit and vegetable prices increased 0.6%, as did dairy prices. Nonalcoholic beverage prices fell 0.3%, while cereal and bakery product prices were unchanged. Those differences explain why individual shopping baskets can move differently from the national average.
Household costs diverge
Monthly change, percent; seasonally adjusted. September → October 2026.
| Component | Sep → Oct | 
|---|---|
| Groceries | −0.1% → 0.4% | 
| All food | 0.0% → 0.5% | 
| Electricity | 0.2% → 0.9% | 
| Piped gas | −0.3% → −0.8% | 
| Shelter | 0.4% → 0.3% | 
| Used vehicles | 0.7% → −1.2% | 
Source: BLS, Table A. As of November 10, 2026.
Shelter inflation slowed to 0.3% from 0.4% but remained a substantial contributor. BLS attributed more than 30% of October’s overall monthly increase to shelter. Used vehicles provided a separate offset, falling 1.2% after rising 0.7% in September. Core goods and services thus included both increases and declines.
The Associated Press reported that headline and core inflation each exceeded forecasts by 0.1 percentage point. It also reported an initial decline in U.S. markets and higher Treasury yields. Those moves show the immediate reaction but do not isolate every influence on asset prices.
Waller said “a stronger policy move may be needed” if core inflation stayed near that monthly pace. Under that condition, he favored considering a half-percentage-point increase in December. His remarks reflect one governor’s preference, not a committee decision or a probability for the outcome.
Annual comparisons are unavailable for most October CPI series. BLS could not collect survey data during October 2025’s funding lapse and therefore cannot publish the corresponding 12-month changes this October. Monthly figures remain available, but September’s annual rate cannot stand in for an unpublished October reading.
Source and evidence matrix
Units: monthly percent changes; policy basis points. Sources dated November 10, 2026.
| Source | Evidence | 
|---|---|
| BLS | Energy: 0.7%; core: 0.3% | 
| Fed / Waller | 50-bp option; conditional | 
| AP | Both prints 0.1 point above forecasts | 
| TS2 calculation | Energy-rate slowdown: 86.5% | 
Calculation: (5.2 − 0.7) ÷ 5.2 × 100. As of November 10, 2026.
Risks: Energy costs could reverse course before the December policy meeting. Monthly seasonal adjustments also mean reported inflation differs from unadjusted pump-price changes. Missing October 2025 data limit annual comparisons, while the next scheduled CPI release comes after the Fed’s decision.
The Fed calendar lists the next meeting for December 8–9. BLS has scheduled November’s CPI for December 10 at 08:30 Eastern time, putting the next consumer-price report one day after the scheduled policy decision.

Expect no Christmas cheer from the Federal Reserve as US inflation comes in hot, warns the CEO of deVere Group, one of the world's largest independent financial advisory organisations.
The comments from Nigel Green come as consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, beating the 0.3% economists had forecast, while core prices, which strip out food and energy, climbed 0.3% for a third consecutive month against expectations of 0.2%.
He says: "These are the inflation numbers nobody wanted to see. Price pressures are digging in across the US economy, and the Fed now has very little room to look the other way."
Hours before the release, Fed Governor Christopher Waller signalled he's leaning towards a December hike, and said a half point move should be considered if core inflation came in around 0.3% or higher. October delivered exactly that.
Markets reacted within minutes. Nasdaq-100 futures fell 1.2%, the two-year Treasury yield jumped more than 15 basis points to almost 4.7%, and the dollar firmed. Traders now see a December hike as a near certainty.
"Markets priced in a hike almost instantly," says Nigel Green. "The question for December 9 is how big it'll be, and how many more follow it into 2027."
The deVere CEO argues October's core reading matters more than the overall figure, because energy has been pulling in the opposite direction. Brent crude slipped below $90 a barrel on Tuesday for the first time since August.
"Oil's been falling and core inflation is still running hot," he says. "Three months of 0.3% works out at an annualised pace of around 3.7%. For a central bank with a 2% target, it's simply too high to ignore."
He adds that the strength of the jobs market gives policymakers cover to act. The US economy added 165,000 jobs in October, more than double forecasts.
"When hiring's this strong, the Fed can tighten without fearing it'll tip the economy over the edge," says Nigel Green. "It's got the justification and the data. Expect it to use both."
Technology shares led the selling, with chipmakers among the hardest hit, while Bitcoin dropped below $73,500 as rate expectations climbed.
"Higher rates bite hardest where valuations lean most heavily on future earnings," he says. "Tech has had a remarkable run on the hope of cheaper money. Investors are now being asked to price in the opposite."
Attention turns next to Friday's wholesale inflation figures, the last major data point before the Fed meets.
"Another hot reading on Friday and a half point move becomes a serious possibility," says Nigel Green.
"Mortgage rates, business loans and government borrowing costs are all likely to stay higher for longer than many households and companies had planned for."
He also sees reasons for optimism amid the tightening.
"Higher yields bring real rewards for savers and income seekers, who are being paid more than they have in years," he says. "And a Fed willing to act decisively now gives it a far better chance of getting inflation under control, which is ultimately good news for markets over the longer term."
He concludes: "Anyone hoping for a festive rate cut can put that wish list away.
"The Fed's message is clear. Inflation is sticky, and it intends to stamp it out.
"Those who plan around higher rates for longer will go into 2027 in far better shape than those still waiting for relief."
