sources.news_title: Hot inflation report puts Fed on track for December rate hike
sources.text:
- Key insight: The latest CPI inflation report, which showed inflation rising 0.4% in October, puts more pressure on the Federal Reserve to increase interest rates. Recent comments suggest policymakers will be ready to hike.
- Expert quote: "I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting. Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take." — Fed Gov. Christopher Waller
Inflation rose faster than expected last month as lower energy costs could not offset broader price increases, according to Tuesday's consumer price index report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, rising 0.4% on the month.
The October CPI reading exceeded the consensus market forecast which expected a monthly increase of 0.24%. The Bureau of Labor Statistics did not issue an October CPI report last year, so the agency did not publish an annualized rate of inflation for last month. The print is better than September, when prices rose 0.6% month over month and 3.7% year over year, but hints at a troubling trend of accelerating inflation.
Ahead of the report, Federal Open Market Committee members were already expressing increased concern about prices. Hours before the report was released, Fed Gov. Christopher Waller said his baseline expectation was that inflation would improve from September but the committee will still raise its benchmark interest rate a quarter percentage point next month.
Even if inflation had come in below 0.3%, Waller said in a pre-written speech delivered in London, he would have backed a 25 basis point hike. With the October reading coming in above that level, he could support a bigger increase.
"I am leaning toward supporting an increase in our policy rate of 25 basis points at the FOMC's December meeting," Waller said. "That's my plan if things proceed as I expect. But if the October CPI inflation data out later today are similar to the past two monthly readings … then a stronger policy move may be needed. In that case, I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting. Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take."
Waller joined the majority of FOMC voters in supporting their move to keep interest rates unchanged during the committee's meeting last month. In his speech he said this was appropriate because the group had already clearly signaled its intent to raise rates repeatedly, enabling market participants to price such a change into their valuation models.
Yet, while the committee bought itself some flexibility in September, Waller said it must follow through on this "sooner rather than later" or else risk losing the trust of financial markets.
Read more:
- OCC: Banks need strong controls when delegating to AI agents
- Democratic wave gives state AGs more enforcement sway
- Midterm drubbing may complicate GOP lame duck priorities
- FDIC taking more piecemeal approach to bank failures
Inflation has been the FOMC's primary concern for months, as price growth from supply-side shocks — including tariffs and the war in Iran — have proven to be persistent. Meanwhile, the Fed's other top priority, maintaining maximum employment, has been firmly in hand. The U.S. economy added 165,000 last month and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%.
Waller is not the only Fed official who has called for tighter monetary policy. Two FOMC participants voted against last month's policy hold, Fed Gov. Lisa Cook and Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack, both of whom preferred a hike.
Cook has yet to explain her rationale. Hammack, in a speech delivered in Zurich, Switzerland last week, noted that inflation has been above the Fed's 2% target for nearly six years and has recently shown signs of broadening out beyond volatile food and energy prices. Because of this, she, too, anticipates monetary policy being tightened.
"I expect that monetary policy will need to move to a restrictive stance to bring inflation back to 2% in a timely manner," Hammack said. "I prefer getting to that stance through more frequent smaller adjustments when possible, something which would be less disruptive to households, businesses, and financial markets."
Two other Fed officials have also signaled that a rate hike is likely on the menu for next month's FOMC meeting.
Richmond Fed President Tom Barkan and Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee both spoke publicly on Monday. Neither called for a rate hike expressly, but both made the case that stable employment, a strong economy and rapidly rising inflation collectively call for raising interest rates.  The two governors will not cast a vote next month, but they will be voting members of the committee next year, beginning in January.
Barkan in a speech delivered in South Carolina, said the right course of action for the Fed was "relatively straightforward," indicating comfort in raising rates. Though he noted that artificial intelligence-driven productivity increases could be a wild card that shifts his thinking. 
"The path of AI feels particularly consequential. If it underdelivers, business investment could pull back, stock prices could follow, and so too could asset-fueled consumer spending," he said. "The risk runs the other way, too. AI could overdeliver and displace more workers than expected, resulting in a pullback in spending. Either scenario would move attention to the maximum employment part of our mandate."
Goolsbee acknowledged the range of long-term implications from AI innovation. However, in the short term, he said the investment boom in the space looks like something the Fed would normally address with higher rates.
"In the Fed world, the bigger the hype, the more nervous I am that we are going to overheat above what the economy is capable of in the next six months," Goolsbee said

sources.news_title: Bitcoin Slips Below $74K as Hot CPI Locks In a Fed Hike
sources.text:
- October inflation came in above forecasts on both the headline and core measures.
- Futures markets now price a December Fed rate hike as close to certain.
- Long-term Bitcoin holders are selling coins below their purchase price.
- Bitcoin trades under both of its main moving averages on the daily chart.
Bitcoin fell below $74,000 on Tuesday after the US Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, a tenth of a point above the consensus forecast, with core inflation also beating expectations at 0.3% against a projected 0.2%. The data pushed the probability of a December rate hike to 98.8% on the CME FedWatch tool, sent Treasury yields and the dollar higher, and hit a crypto market where long-term holders had already started selling at a loss.
A 0.4% print the Fed cannot look past
Core CPI strips out food and energy, the two most volatile categories, so the Federal Reserve treats it as the cleaner signal of whether price pressure is spreading through the economy. A 0.3% monthly core reading works out to roughly 3.7% on an annualized basis, well above the central bank’s 2% target, and that gap between the core figure and the target is what moved rates traders on Tuesday.
The release also came without its usual headline number. The BLS said it will not publish year-over-year figures for October because the agency never collected prices in October 2025, when the federal government shutdown halted its survey work. With no base month to compare against, the monthly change became the only official measure of inflation for the period, and markets weighed it accordingly.
Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller added to the pressure, saying he wants a hike in December and is open to a 50 basis point move, which means raising the policy rate by half a percentage point in one step instead of the usual quarter point. With a hike almost fully priced, the market’s attention has moved to its size.
How a hot CPI number travels into crypto
Higher expected rates feed into Bitcoin through a few connected channels. Rising Treasury yields increase what investors give up by holding an asset that pays no interest, and a stronger dollar tightens financial conditions for buyers outside the US who fund positions in dollars. Leveraged traders in crypto futures feel it fastest, because higher rates push up the cost of keeping positions open and falling prices can force liquidations. The same rate repricing hit equities, which tend to move with Bitcoin when expectations for Fed policy shift sharply.
Long-term holders sell below cost for eight straight days
The macro shock arrived while on-chain data already showed stress among Bitcoin’s most patient investors. According to analyst Axel Adler Jr., LTH-SOPR has stayed below 1 for eight consecutive days. The metric compares the price at which long-term holders, defined as wallets holding coins for more than 155 days, sell their coins with the price they originally paid. A reading below 1 means that, on average, those coins changed hands at a loss.
Adler noted that similar readings appeared several times over the past year, but the indicator just posted one of its sharpest monthly drops of 2026, and it was the speed of that move that stood out to him. A large share of long-term supply was bought during the 2025 run above $100,000, so even a price in the mid-$70,000 range leaves those holders underwater.
The size of that cohort is shrinking as well. Adler’s LTH supply data shows 16.3 million BTC held by long-term holders, down 171,700 BTC over the past month. He cautioned that coins also enter this group simply by aging past the 155-day threshold, so the figure can move without any purchase or sale. A net decline means long-term holders spent more coins than the aging process added to the group over the month.

Altcoins absorbed heavier losses than Bitcoin over the week, with XRP down almost 17% and Hyperliquid’s HYPE token off nearly 14% even as Hyperliquid Strategies pursues a US futures broker license, and the total crypto market value slipped to $2.48 trillion, while the CMC Crypto Fear and Greed Index fell to 27.
The index peaked at 82 on August 27 and bottomed at 5 on February 6, so the current reading still sits well above this year’s panic low.
Bitcoin loses the 200-day average it reclaimed in September
On the daily Binance chart, Bitcoin trades near $73,950, down 1.87% on the session, after briefly touching $73,525. Price now sits below the 200-day exponential moving average at $76,475, a line many traders use to separate long-term uptrends from downtrends, and below the 50-day average at $79,110, which has started to turn lower.
The two averages formed a golden cross in mid-September, when the shorter one moved above the longer one and the rally toward $87,000 followed. That gap has narrowed to about $2,600. If the 50-day keeps falling toward the 200-day, the setup would reverse into a death cross, a signal that tends to attract trend-following sellers. The MACD momentum indicator also remains below its signal line, with both values deep in negative territory, a reading that has stayed negative since late October without any sign of a turn.
Recent candles left long lower wicks near $73,000, showing where buyers stepped in over the past few sessions. On the way up, the first test is the 200-day average around $76,500, followed by the 50-day near $79,100.
Waller’s 50 bps remark puts hike size on the table
A quarter-point hike in December is already in prices, so a move of that size would add little new pressure on its own. The real risk for crypto and equities is a half-point increase or a signal from the Fed that further hikes will follow in early 2027, and Waller’s comments make that outcome harder to dismiss. On the on-chain side, a return of LTH-SOPR above 1 would show that long-term holders have stopped selling at a loss, while a pause in the LTH supply decline would suggest the distribution from older wallets is easing.
The next CPI report should restore the full picture. The BLS did collect price data in November 2025 after the shutdown ended, which means the November 2026 release will carry an annual inflation rate again, and it will be the first official year-over-year figure since September that traders and Fed officials can compare against the 2% target.

Bitcoin Price Dips Under $74,000 as CPI Prints 0.4%: Key Levels
Bitcoin slipped below $74,000 on Tuesday as October's inflation report showed core prices rising at the same pace for a third month, leaving the daily candle just above its 200-day average.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, after a 0.6% increase in September, with the index excluding food and energy up 0.3%.
The number that matters is the one that didn’t move
The headline figure cooled from September, but the part of the report the Federal Reserve watches most closely did not. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, printed 0.3% in October, exactly as it did in September and August. Three months at that pace work out to roughly 3.7% a year, close to double the Fed’s 2% target, and the stability of the number is itself the message: nothing in October suggests the underlying rate is slowing.
Shelter did most of the lifting. It rose 0.3% and accounted for more than thirty percent of the monthly increase, with owners’ equivalent rent up 0.3% and rent up 0.2%. Food climbed 0.5%, its sharpest monthly rise since April, driven by a 0.9% jump in beef and a 1.0% rise in snacks. Energy added 0.7% after September’s 5.2% surge, and gasoline is up 37.4% over twelve months on an unadjusted basis. The few declines came from used cars, down 1.2%, and communication services.
One figure is absent. The BLS collected no data in October 2025 during last year’s lapse in appropriations, so it cannot publish a twelve-month change for the all-items index this month. Traders who usually anchor on the annual rate were left with the monthly sequence alone: 0.4%, 0.6%, 0.4% for headline and 0.3%, 0.3%, 0.3% for core.
Why bitcoin took it badly
A report that keeps core inflation stuck at 0.3% a month is a report that gives the Fed no reason to ease faster, and bitcoin has spent this cycle trading as a bet on cheaper money. That was the macro backdrop at 8:30 ET. The chart, though, was already in trouble before the release, and the inflation print landed on a market that had failed the same level three days running.
Three failed sessions at the 0.382
For three sessions the daily candles had been probing the underside of the 0.382 Fibonacci level near $76,066, a line that held as support through the October range and flipped into resistance once it broke. Each wick was turned back without a close above it.
Tuesday’s candle opened at $75,368, reached an intraday high of $75,442, then sold off to $73,525 before stabilising. At $73,904 the pair is down $1,465, or 1.94%, on the day, and the move has carried price out of the band that contained last week’s pullback.
Where the drop stopped
The intraday low came $333 above the rising purple 200-day simple moving average at $73,191. Directly beneath it, only $630 lower, sits the horizontal 0.500 Fibonacci midpoint around $72,561. Together they form a floor the daily chart has not tested since the September breakout lifted price out of the $64,000 to $69,000 base.
Momentum arrived there already stretched. The daily RSI (14) reads 34.24, under its 38.46 signal line and approaching the 30 threshold that marks oversold territory. Volume on the session was 7.22K BTC, in line with recent days rather than the kind of spike that usually marks a capitulation low.
Distance from $73,904
The ceiling has moved down
Any recovery now has to clear two layers that were support a fortnight ago. The first is the 0.382, which has just rejected three attempts. The second is the red 100-day SMA at $77,575, which price cut through on Monday without a pause. Higher still, the yellow 50-day SMA at $81,451 is curving lower above the 0.236 Fibonacci near $80,403, so even a strong bounce would meet a falling average before it met the old range highs.
Two ways the next sessions can go
If the floor holds. A daily close that defends the 0.500 and 200-day zone, with RSI this close to oversold, sets up the conditions for a relief bounce back toward $76,066. That level is where the bounce gets graded: a close above it would put the 100-day SMA back on the map; another rejection would confirm the lower ceiling.
If the floor fails. A decisive daily close beneath $72,561 surrenders both the 200-day SMA and the macro midpoint in one move. Below that, the chart has no horizontal level until the 0.618 retracement, often called the golden pocket, close to $69,056, which also marks the top of the September breakout candle. That is a further 6.6% from Tuesday’s price, and RSI would be deep in oversold territory before it got there.
What to watch
Bitcoin has spent two months inside a range drawn by the Fibonacci levels of its summer run, and Tuesday’s drop took it to the lower half of that range rather than out of it. The next inflation reading, November’s CPI, is scheduled for December 10. Until then, the daily closes relative to $73,191 below and $76,066 above decide whether this was a dip to support or the start of a deeper retracement.

US core CPI rose 0.3% mom in October for a third consecutive month, exceeding expectations of 0.2% and underscoring persistent underlying inflation pressures. Headline CPI moderated from 0.6% mom to 0.4%, but also exceeded the 0.3% consensus. The divergence reflects a sharp slowdown in energy inflation that helped contain the overall index, while price pressures across several services categories continued to resist moderation. The failure of core CPI to ease suggests that underlying disinflation has yet to regain convincing momentum, despite the improvement in headline inflation.
Within the core index, services inflation outside housing remained a notable source of pressure. Services excluding rent of shelter accelerated from 0.3% to 0.5%, even as shelter inflation slowed from 0.4% to 0.3%. Transportation services inflation increased from 0.6% to 0.8%, including a rise in motor vehicle insurance from 0.1% to 0.7%. Recreation prices accelerated from 0.5% to 0.8%, while medical care inflation rose from 0.1% to 0.3%, with hospital services increasing 0.8%. Goods prices provided some offsetting relief, as core commodities inflation eased from 0.3% to 0.2%, helped by used-car prices falling 1.2% after rising 0.7% in September. However, improvements in shelter and goods were insufficient to reduce overall core inflation.
Headline inflation slowed primarily as energy price increases moderated sharply. The energy index rose 0.7% in October after surging 5.2% in September, while gasoline inflation eased from 9.1% to 1.0%. Electricity prices increased 0.9%, although natural gas prices declined 0.8%. Meanwhile, food inflation accelerated from 0.0% to 0.5%, partly offsetting the energy relief. Grocery prices rose 0.4%, while food away from home increased 0.5%, including a 0.7% rise in full-service restaurant meals. Shelter also contributed more than 30% of the monthly headline CPI increase despite its slower rate of growth. The composition indicates that the headline moderation was concentrated in energy, rather than reflecting a broad-based easing in consumer prices.
October’s figures leave the underlying inflation outlook uncertain. Three consecutive monthly core readings of 0.3% suggest that price pressures are proving more persistent than markets anticipated, particularly across non-housing services. Earlier on Tuesday, Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller warned that a 50bps December rate hike should be considered if core CPI remained around 0.3% mom or higher, although his remarks preceded the release and do not establish the Fed’s eventual response. The Bureau of Labor Statistics was also unable to publish most October year-on-year CPI changes because October 2025 index data were unavailable following the government funding lapse. For now, the monthly figures provide a clear distinction: headline inflation is cooling as energy pressures ease, but core inflation has not yet demonstrated a sustained improvement.

| Headline CPI (mom) | 0.4% | 0.3% | 0.6% |

All changes are seasonally adjusted month-on-month. October annual CPI rates are largely unavailable because corresponding October 2025 indexes were not published.
Key Takeaways
- US core CPI held at 0.3% mom for a third consecutive month, exceeding expectations of 0.2%, while headline inflation slowed from 0.6% to 0.4% but also beat forecasts.
- Non-housing services inflation remained persistent, with services excluding rent of shelter accelerating from 0.3% to 0.5%, offsetting easing shelter and core goods prices.
- Energy inflation slowed sharply from 5.2% to 0.7%, helping headline CPI moderate, but food inflation accelerated from 0.0% to 0.5%, leaving underlying disinflation unconvincing.

October Inflation Runs Hotter Than Expected, Renewing Pressure on Mortgage Rates
U.S. inflation rises more than expected as prices climb
sources.text:
(AP) — U.S. inflation was higher than expected last month as the rising prices that powered sweeping Democratic victories in last week’s midterm elections appear likely to pose ongoing challenges for the White House and the Federal Reserve.
The consumer price index rose 0.4% from September to October, the Labor Department said Tuesday, down from 0.6% the previous month. The government did not report a yearly inflation rate because last year’s government shutdown meant no data was released for October 2025.
But excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 0.3%, the same as the preceding month. Both figures were a tenth of a point higher than forecast, and at an annual rate would be well above the Fed’s 2% target.
The new inflation data heightened concerns that strong consumer and business spending, combined with higher gas prices and supply disruptions stemming from tariffs and global turmoil, are creating increasingly stubborn inflation that could extend beyond temporary spikes in prices at the gas pump. The economy expanded at a 3.4% annual rate in the July-September quarter, mostly driven by consumer spending.
“It’s worrisome. There is a sense that inflation is broad, persistent, a little bit everywhere,” said Riccardo Trezzi, founder of Underlying Inflation, a consulting firm, and a former Fed economist. “The Fed should be very worried.”
Using rough estimates for last October’s data, Trezzi calculates that consumer prices rose 4% in October from a year ago, up from 3.7% in September. Core prices rose 2.8%, he estimates, up from 2.6%.
Americans’ struggles with high prices were evident as they ousted Republican majorities from the House and Senate last week. With historic gains in both chambers, Democrats in Congress will soon face the same challenges.
President Donald Trump has acknowledged voter anger over the Iran war and gas prices but has shown no sign yet of changing course.
The AP Voter Poll, a survey of 100,000 voters, found about two-thirds blamed Trump’s policies for higher costs. About 9 in 10 said the cost of living was a “crucial” or “major” factor in their vote.
Federal Reserve may become more aggressive about raising borrowing costs
The persistence of elevated inflation makes it highly likely that the Fed will raise its key interest rate at its next meeting in December. It kept rates unchanged late last month, after raising them in September. The Fed increases borrowing costs in an effort to cool spending and bring down inflation.
Earlier Tuesday, Fed governor Christopher Waller, an outspoken member of the central bank’s rate-setting committee, said that a hike of a half-point next month was possible, double the size of the usual quarter-point increase.
“Economic activity is strong, the labor market is stable, but inflation is too high, well above” the Fed’s 2% goal, Waller said.
Stock prices fell in early trading Tuesday, and Treasury yields rose, on expectations of more persistent inflation and higher rates from the Fed.
Higher gas prices may have begun to spread through economy
Gas prices rose 1% from September to October, the government said, a stiff increase but still much lower than in previous months. Gas prices have soared more than 37% from a year ago. Still, oil prices have fallen sharply in recent days on hopes that the Iran conflict is fading, and gas costs have declined this month.
Yet there are signs higher energy prices are spreading into other parts of the economy, with air fares, public transportation, and delivery services all jumping in price. Electricity prices rose 0.9% from September to October, the most since April, and grocery prices jumped 0.4%, a painful rise after years of increases.
Beef prices rose 0.9% last month, after jumping nearly 14% in the first half of this year. Restaurant prices rose 0.5% from September to October, the most since January 2024. Rising shipping prices, driven up by more expensive gas, have lifted costs for restaurants and grocery stores, which may be passing them on to consumers.
Inflation has also been worsened by the massive investments flowing into artificial intelligence, which has contributed to higher prices for computer chips, electricity and consumer electronics. Voters swept dozens of candidates into office who had pledged to slow data center construction.
Computer prices jumped 0.5% last month, the government report showed, after rising nearly 10% in the year ending in September, lifted by more expensive chips. The cost of computers had been retreating for years as semiconductor chips became more efficient. That trend reversed course this year as prices rose sharply.
Prices are rising, and it’s not just gasoline
Prices are also rising in some sectors that have little to do with oil and gas or AI. Streaming video services have recently gotten more expensive, with Disney raising prices last month for its ad-supported Disney+ and Hulu streaming bundle to $12.49 a month from $11.99. The ad-free version rose by $2.50 to $21.49.
Prices also increased last month for an Apple TV/Peacock streaming bundle, to $17.99 from $14.99 a month.
Small businesses are bracing for a spending pullback by customers.
Chris Butler, CEO of National Tree Company, an artificial tree importer and wholesaler, says most of his customers now spend $200 or less on a tree. That is a big departure from the pandemic days when many people, flush with cash, were spending $300 to $400, he said.
“Inflation continues to persist,” he said. “Gas prices continue to be high, so consumers are hurting from a discretionary perspective.”
Last year, National Tree was forced to raise prices on its products, sourced in China and Cambodia, between 10% and 15% because of Trump’s tariffs, Butler said. Tariffs have come down, but now the firm is grappling with higher diesel costs.
Butler said the company, based in Cranford, N.J., doesn’t plan to raise prices again this year given the existing financial stress on customers, who are already spending less on trees.
Outside of inflation, other measures show the economy is largely doing well. The unemployment rate is a low 4.1% and growth is steady. Still, high prices have left most Americans with a dour view of the economy.
“It might not be a recession, but if you’re still living paycheck to paycheck and watching gas prices go up, grocery prices go up, your rent costs go up, it’s not going to feel like a robust economy,” said Jim Baird, chief investment officer at Plante Moran Financial Advisors.
___
AP Retail Writer Anne D’Innocenzio in New York contributed to this story.
